Mr. ANDREW McMASTER (Brome) moved concurrence of the House in the fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh reports of the committee charged with the investigation into agricultural conditions in Canada.
He said: I would just like to ask the House to grant me permission to postpone any remarks I have to offer until I see whether the reports are open to criticism. I take it that informally moving the concurrence of the House in these reports I do not exhaust my right to speak.
Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader
of the Opposition): I do not know what the object would be of the House adopting now four reports just recently presented, certainly ill-digested, so far as the House is concerned, if digested or read at all. If legislation is contemplated this session, then there would be some object in a discussion now of the merits of the reports. But if no legislation is in view-and we had the intimation yesterday there was not-it seems to me that we are not using very well the short time that remains in discussing these four reports. I do not make these remarks in any spirit of antagonism to the reports, because I am frank to admit I am doubtful whether I have read them all. I know I have read a good deal of them; but I venture to say that a great number, if not the vast majority in this House, have not read any part of them. I would think it would be better to defer consideration of them, until we were in a position to legislate, if legislation was thought desirable. We are not in such a position now.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee on Bill No. 222, to amend the Dominion Lands Act, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 2-Transfer of holders of letters patent in pre-emption and purchased homestead area to another homestead, by provincial certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the request of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), this clause stood, and I did not make any explanation at the time in connection with it. The explanation is that for some considerable time, the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have made representations asking that individuals who have homesteaded in the southern areas known as the drier areas of those provinces be given the privilege of securing a second homestead if they were desirous of doing so, in the northern area of the particular province, where more fertile lands were available. To meet this, we have embodied in this clause a provision that where an individual has had a homestead and has made failure owing to no fault of his own, but rather to climatic conditions that exist in those areas, he be given an opportunity to take a homestead in the northern area of the province under the provisions of the Dominion Lands Act. It is necessary that he be armed with the certificate from the provincial government showing that in their opinion he is entitled to consideration. We have confined this matter to the area south of township 31, not including all the district formerly known as the pre-emption area across the two provinces. That is all we propose to do in the matter. I may assure the committee that we propose to make a careful inquiry to make sure that we are not being imposed upon, and to confine our operations absolutely to those who have been unsuccessful in this particular area.
How does the minister intend to dispose of the lands that are being vacated?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the land owned by the individual is unencumbered it will revert to the Crown. This section is designed to cover the case of the individual who has failed in due course and loses the land he homesteaded within the boundary described in this section.

Dominion Lands Act
If the original homestead is mortgaged does the government propose to assume the obligations in respect of that land?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

How is it intended to meet such a situation? If the land reverts to the government, I presume from the minister's answer, it will be unencumbered, but what about the homestead on which there is a mortgage?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no difficulty in relation to the man whose title is clear; but the government will certainly not assume the obligations on encumbered property.
I should hope not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is
rather for the purpose of assisting the individual who has failed and who has to surrender his homestead. If a man loses his homestead by mortgage or otherwise, we do not assume the responsibility for those obligations, but we assist him to settle in the northern portion of the province rather than have him go out of the country altogether, as unfortunately too many do. A large number of men in such circumstances go South, and this is intended to retain them in Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I certainly favour the
working out of a plan for granting second homesteads or, in other words, giving a second opportunity to those who are in the dry areas. The opening up of these dry areas was one among other mistakes of the former government -I mean the next antecedent one in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was then in the same office. The lands were opened up for homesteading when they should not have been, and they have been a source of disappointment and penury ever since. I realize the minister's difficulty in now trying to find some remedy for the consequences of that mistake, but while I fully appreciate that difficulty I do not think he has met it very well. The hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) mentioned a point which, in my judgment, is not as important as another one that I shall suggest later on. Still it has not been answered. Suppose a man has his homestead in the dry area and* it is'mortgaged-this can be taken to be the normal condition, for I fancy that if the homestead were not mortgaged that would indicate that the party could not get a mortgage on it; such has been the history of the district, the man would be compelled to mortgage the property if he could-we assume,
therefore, that the homestead is mortgaged. This, of course, puts a premium on the individual's leaving and going North. The Government does not get his homestead; it certainly cannot step in and defeat the mortgagee of whatever asset he has in the homestead, little as it may be. Consequently the land will simply be foreclosed and become the property of the mortgagee. The difference between the man who has his land clear and the man who has not such a title to it is that in the one case the government gets the land and in the other the mortgagee gets it. I presume the minister intends to let the fellow with the mortgage have a second homestead, because if he does not then the legislation might as well be wiped out; for I should think that nearly all the homesteads would be mortgaged, and those who hav$ mortgaged and failed are those who need the second homestead. The minister has not said whether he purposes to let those whose land is mortgaged get a second homestead. If he does he is putting the country in the position of losing the first homestead altogether and turning it over to the mortgagee.
The second point is this. It is stated that any one can get a second homestead who has a certificate from the provincial government showing that he has failed at farming througl no fault of his own but through adverse cir cumstances. But the minister has his officer! all through the districts; he has homestead inspectors1-and I can remember some of the criticism that was offered in regard to the number of them when the vote to pay them was passed. Why should they not report on the condition and history of these homesteads? Why should the provincial government be asked to give any certificate? The provincial government will simply have to appoint another set of officers, putting additional taxation on the people; no other result can follow. They will be obliged to have another set of homestead inspectors to examine all these cases and that means a squadron of them. But even aside from the question of expense to the public, which will be very considerable, it is not right for one government to rest on the responsibility of another, it is not consistent with our system of government at all. This government should use its own judgment on the advice of its officers in this matter as in anything of a similar nature. I suggest to the minister, therefore, that he wipe out that provision. I would rather s'ee something done that removes the question of discretion altogether; in fact I think that otherwise the minister will get into interminable wrangles and utterly ines-
Dominion Lands Act

capable conditions of unfairness and partiality. He cannot help it. Throughout the length and breadth of the country farmers can be selected in hundreds, yes, thousands, who have failed, not through any fault of their own at all, and not in this particular area. Farmers all over Canada have failed because of continual visitations of drought, continual visitations of hail and frost and one misfortune or another; and what answer can the minister give those men who come and say that they are just as entitled to relief as the farmers over there to the west? They will say, " You give relief to these men on this especial ground; very well, apply it to us in the same way." And what answer can the minister give? I have not the least doubt, although none of this area is in the province of Manitoba, that the Manitoba government could certify to hundreds and thousands who have failed through no fault of their own, who perhaps succeeded for a time and now are worth nothing. How can the minister refuse them new homesteads? On these grounds I do not think the minister's relief is an efficient working out of the problem. In my judgment it would have been better to have simply declared certain areas to be homestead areas and then said to those men: Select new homesteads there. In this case, I am free to admit, there would be some unfairness to those outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You would have exactly the same difficulty.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, because those are areas that never should have been opened. And you do not rest upon the favour of a provincial government, you rest simply upon the cold, bald fact that areas were opened that should not have been opened, and you say to the men who went in there "Go and take homesteads somewhere else." Let me repeat; I object to a government shifting its responsibility on to another government. Let it take its own responsibility. But I am free to admit that if ever a government should shift responsibility it is this one.

The debate so far has brought up a question which I imagine will be discussed on the adoption of the report of the Agricultural Conditions committee-the creation of a national land bank for the relief of the farmers of the West. If that is so, there will have to be some discussion later on in regard to it, and perhaps the Government will announce a policy which, besides allowing farmers to re-homestead, will give them a measure of relief such as the farmers have in the United States,

through a national bank credit system with the credit of the nation behind it. So this is only a partial measure. It must go further, it must be supplemented by giving the farmer a better system of credit. This bill really ignores the main issue, which is a land bank system similar to what they have adopted in the United States to enable the farmer to get on his feet financially. We ought to have such a system in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would remind my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) that this is not a question of banking.
It is.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon, it is a question of giving relief to certain areas, whereas the question of banking would cover the whole Dominion.
My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) states that there are certain well defined areas on which we should offer individuals another choice of a free homestead to give them a fresh start. There is absolutely not a particle of difference in the proposal embodied in this section and what he suggested a moment ago in criticism of this bill. We are told that mistakes were made by former governments. Well, I do not know whether we should criticise former governments for what the3' have done in this respect. I know I have had a good deal of anxiety in regard to the southern area of Alberta and that in all efforts to alleviate the distress of the people in that territory the two governments have worked hand in hand. It is not suggested that we should put upon the provincial government the responsibility of saying who shall and who shall not have homesteads, but inasmuch as the western provinces are claiming their natural resources, we thought it only right that if any individual was to be given a homestead the provincial government should be informed of the fact. It is for this reason that the provincial government is being brought into the matter at all.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the reason?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In every
effort that has been made for the alleviation of distress in these areas the two governments have acted together, practically.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I beg my right hon. friend's pardon. As an instance, take the distribution of seed grain.

Dominion Lands Act

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The two governments have co-operated, I do not object to that; but the Dominion government never acted on the responsibility of the provincial government. The Dominion government, for example, did not give seed grain relief to a man recommended for it by the provincial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I beg my right hon. friend's pardon, they did.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They did it in Alberta. The practice has been followed for the last six years. Not only that, but relief has been distributed by the provincial officers to the homesteaders.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That may be, but the provincial government does it on its own responsibility. We did not make a condition that the man should be recommended by the provincial government, we took the responsibility ourselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the result of what you did do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, it is not. I think I ought to know.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For instance, by whose authority did you advance seed grain to a homesteader? True, the provincial government were advancing it to those with unpatented land, but you took the word of the provincial officer, you advanced the amount of grain, your own officer purchased the grain and put it in your elevators. I know what I am talking about.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No. If the minister looks at the law he will see he is mistaken. I administered the act and know what was done. We decided on our own responsibility whether an unpatented homesteader needed seed grain or not, we did not rely upon the recommendation of the provincial government. We made arrangements by passing legislation providing that the banks should advance the money in the first place and we guaranteed five per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So did the province.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Very well. That shows we did not collect it through the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Every application passed through the hands of the provincial authorities. I am speaking of the practice in recent years.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It was not the practice under me.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But that is aside from the question. By this clause it is simply intended that the provincial government shall be consulted and that we shall . accept their certificate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But you cannot grant a homestead without their certificate.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are
anxious to have their co-operation to clean up a very difficult situation. I admit everything my right hon. friend has said about the difficulty. It would be very much easier for the government not to do anything at all- and perhaps it would be fairer taking all things into consideration. The very fact that a person who has selected land in this particular territory has made a failure-I admit my right hon. friend's argument-is not a good reason why he should be given a preference over the man who has tried in some other territory and has made a like failure. But we have a difficult situation to deal with. I am not unmindful of the difficulties at all, I see every one of those presented by my right hon. friend, but rather than have the people across the line we thought it well to devise ways and means to enable them to make a fresh start in the northern portion of the province if they were desirous of going there. And if any individual is to be given a privilege, it seems only reasonable that the provincial authorities should at least be consulted in the matter.
Not that they are to step in and shoulder any of our responsibility. We are not delegating any of our responsibility to the provincial government. My own idea with respect to the settlement of this vexed question would be if possible to move the settlers off these very dry areas and return these areas again to ranching lands. In doing that, of course, regard must be had to obligations that are already upon the lands-mortgage obligations, school bonds, and so on. I am speaking now of lands which cannot be irrigated. There is a demand that the department try to solve the problem and we are prepared to make an effort. I do not anticipate that a very large number of people will take advantage of the legislation. For instance, a man who has a mortgage on his land is not going to relinquish that land unless he thinks there is no chance of his making good. It is my experience, after eight years of intimate knowledge of the conditions affecting the people who live in these localities, that they invari-
Dominion Lands Act

ably stay until they have to leave-and their leaving means that there is no equity left in the property at all.

I am veiy glad indeed that the minister has undertaken to solve this very difficult problem; it has been a nightmare to banks, merchants and provincial and federal governments for some time. Undoubtedly there are areas that should never have been taken from the rancher-good ranching districts that were destroyed to make a very poor farming district. In 1914 I had occasion to travel over some five hundred miles of this dry area for the purpose of gathering some information and looking into the facts. You will remember that 1914 was a very dry season, but some of the farmers in that district had good crops. I inquired why it was that one farmer had a good crop while perhaps fifty or one hundred round about had nothing, and I found that the men on the farms that had given a good return had been doing their work in a scientific way and had conserved all the moisture that was humanly possible to conserve. Now, it might appear from that experience that the difference was simply a case of good farming as against poor farming, but I believe that is not so. The year 1914 followed several comparatively wet years, and there was some moisture to conserve. Subsequently there were a number of dry years-up to two years ago we had had four or five dry years- with the result that there was no moisture to conserve; the subsoil was as dry as powder. That leads me to believe that in these dry areas, no matter how well the soil is farmed, it is impossible to attain success. A great many of the people who settled in those districts came in with considerable amount of money; their buildings are comparatively new and in many instances are better buildings than those we find in the older areas. For that reason I think it is well that opportunity should be given to those who wish to do so to move to areas where they can succeed.
With a part of what the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) said I must agree, namely, that it would be wiser to base any action taken on the conditions affecting each individual farmer in the area in which he resides. If it is simply a case of the farmer failing through no fault of his own, why, you would have applications made from all over the country. But the difference is this:	Many farmers are living on
land where, if the economic conditions were made right, they could succeed. They are 
living on land that can be profitably worked and which can reasonably be expected in the future to yield a fair return. On the other hand, those who live in these arid districts are on land where no farmer, be he ever so good, could possibly succeed. In 1915 the crop in these arid districts was an [DOT] enormous one, perhaps the greatest that western Canada ever saw-fifty, and even sixty bushels to the acre being not uncommon. The extent of the crop was almost unbelievable. And perhaps that was one of the worst things that could have happened to some of the farmers there, because it gave them hope; they believed they could go to almost any extent in their schemes of expansion, and they hung on year after year for three or four or five years. If another good crop comes, the same thing will happen again, but any temporary measure of success in a given year simply prolongs the agony. It does seem to me that farmers living in these arid districts where it will always be impossible for them to succeed should be entitled to a new homestead, if they take it within a specified time. Of course, the door should not be left open, after this regulation is passed, to those living in other parts of the country to move to another homestead after they have tried one in the arid district for say six months. It should apply, however, to those who settled in these arid districts in good faith. The minister has said he does not think that very many are likely to take advantage of this opportunity. Well, the reason for that is not that the chances of success under their present conditions are good, but simply that they have invested their all. To my mind they would be well advised to take advantage of this opportunity and accept new homesteads.

I hestitate to criticise
this legislation, because I suppose it applies to all the prairie provinces, but I doubt whether it is going to be very beneficial to the province with which I am best acquainted, Alberta. It seems to me that this is the way it will work out: Four or five of these homesteaders will go up in the north part of the province and get a desirable piece of land; then they will get after the provincial government for schools and after the municipality for roads, and neither of these organizations will be prepared to accede to their requests. I do not think there is any need for the adoption of this course. I am quite convinced that these people could go up to that north country and either buy or rent land much cheaper than they could get a homestead to-day. The legislation may be all right theoretically, but I very much doubt whether

Board of Audit
it will work out when an attempt is made to put it into practice. I would also point out to the minister that the day cannot be much longer delayed when he will have to give consideration to the demand for the return to the western provinces of their natural resources. Every acre that the government disposes of will simply add to the barrier existing between the Dominion government and the provinces -when that day of reckoning comes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will tell us how close that " day of reckoning " is that the hon. member refers to.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
So far as
the minister is concerned it might happen tomorrow. I am not, however, speaking for the government in that regard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is just as likely to
happen to-morrow as it was eighteen months ago.
Bill reported, read the third time and
passed.

maintopic: BOUNTIES ON COPPER BARS OR RODS
speechtext:
I beg in connection
with clause 3 to move an amendment by adding a clause 3A. I regret that I have not had an opportunity to prepare a copy for the Minister of Finance, but I will send over my original to him forthwith.
I am utterly opposed to this bounty business. I think it is eminently unsound. I think the business men who want to start business in this country, if they have got a meritorious proposition should reap the benefits and run the risks. In this case we encourage people to ask the state to help. The state runs the risk while others receive all the benefits. That being the case I move:
That the following paragraph be added to paragraph 3 to be known as paragraph 3A:
3A. Any amount so paid out shall be considered as advances by way of loan to those receiving the same and shall be repayable to the Crown as follows: One-fifth of the amount received on the 1st

This is the situation in connection with the copper industry and something should be done to meet it. The raw copper of British Columbia goes to-day to the United States, where a large quantity is required. It is refined there and we buy it back again. That is a condition of things which even free traders would not, I suppose, care to have continue. We have an abundant supply of raw copper in this country, but the new companies that undertake to develop this industry cannot stand up against the outside competition of old and well-established businesses in a country like the United States. Concerning any other question there might be greater room for differences of opinion; but this is a case in which we are developing an industry that gets its raw material from the bowels of the earth, that raw material being of no value in its undeveloped state. I think, therefore, that it is well that we should do something to develop this potential asset. I believe in aiding this industry, which has for its object the development of one of our greatest national assets in the way of natural products. Under the present law, a manufacturer, say, of copper bars, can get his raw material free of duty, but if he attempts to manufacture a partly finished product to a further stage and sell it to his neighbour in Canada, though that neighbour lives across the street, he has to pay a duty on his importation. I cannot see anything inconsistent with straight business methods in doing what the government proposes to do in order that the copper industry of Canada may be developed, and those who are manufacturing further products of the copper mines may be given a chance at least equal to that enjoyed by the American who can send in his goods now free of charge.

I became somewhat familiar with this matter about two or three years ago. I do not think there is any dispute that it does seem to be ridiculous that the brass manufacturer-the man who is manufacturing the product of the copper- although he uses Canadian copper, as a result of the present protective tariff-which in this instance is not protective at all but is a tax upon the Canadian producer-is worse off than if he moved his plant to Buffalo. That is, as a result of the duty on the raw material of copper, given for the purpose of aiding the first industry, the production of copper itself, unaccompanied by proper compensatory duties upon the more finished article, while it gives an apparent protective duty of 10 per cent to the brass manufacturer, it actually leaves him at a disadvantage of 2 per cent. Therefore, although we have a duty on the raw material, we are getting the benefit of the first process only, the extraction of the copper from the ground. Those were the figures two years ago, and I am quite confident they are the figures to-day. Consequently, where we ought to have large employment of labour in connection with all the different processes of this industry, we are just simply producing the raw material. I take it that my hon. friend has had those figures before him and has calculated what he could do in order to offset the difference.
I might say that the result of it all comes from an accident. Things are overlooked from time to time. There used to be no duty whatever upon the by-products of copper. We had no industry in connection with them. When the war came we had to have these by-products. There was no competition when the industry started and those engaged in it had the further protection given by the 7| per cent customs tax imposed for war purposes. It is by reason of the tax being cancelled that we are in this position to-day, because while reductions have been made on the import duties, on the other hand the striking off of that tax, which before gave the industry a net protection of 5 per cent, leaves it in a position where it is at a disadvantage to the extent of from 2 to 2| per cent. I do not think there is very much doubt about these figures. Of course, I should like to see the fullest information given, but, speaking frankly, I can see absolutely no reason why this industry should not be bonused.

The object of this bill is to establish in western Canada very largely and in the province of Manitoba particularly, I believe a new industry for the growing of hemp and its manufacture into binder twine. I understand that an experienced man from the north of Ireland, where this industry has been developed as highly probably as in any other part of the world, came to Canada some years ago and made investigations as to the possibility of growing this hemp in Manitoba. I understand that it was established to his entire satisfaction that hemp of the very finest quality could be grown there, of a quality equal to that which the factories in the north of Ireland had been purchasing from Russia before the war. Hemp has been grown in the West for some three years. I have seen it growing, and while I do not know anything about its quality I know that it grows very readily and very high. I have been assured by this gentleman from Ireland that this hemp is of the very best quality and will produce the very finest twine when manufactured. Another feature of the situation is that the twine which we use in Canada is very largely manufactured outside of Canada, manufactured practically by one company ,the International Harvester Company, a large American corporation with a vast capital. Twine has gone up in western Canada to a very high and unusual price, and is more or less absolutely in the control of this company. The object of this bill is to create a new industry. I agree that there is a proper place for_ the granting of bounties and subsidies. This is a new concern with a reasonable prospect of being successful. I would be opposed to the granting of a bounty if there was not a reasonable prospect of success.

May I ask a question?
If there is a reasonable chance of success why should it be objected to that the industry should repay to the state the amount which the state is now advancing to it?

I will answer my hon. friend as I proceed with my argument. We have western Canada in the grip of this monopoly I spoke of. We have a field out

Bounty on Hemp
there for the building up of a magnificent industry. We have a large market in western Canada for binder twine, one of the largest markets in the world. The great trouble with our manufactures in Canada has been that their market has been limited as compared with the United States, and for that reason on account of the greater overhead expense they were unable to compete with the American factories. But for this binder twine industry we should have a field as large as that of the United States, and one in which we can compete against them successfully. There is I think no doubt at all that this industry will succeed if the bounty is large enough in the first instance to enable them to compete against this monopoly that now holds the people of western Canada in thrall.
The establishment of such an industry should have the following effects: First there should be a reduction in the price of twine for the farmers of western Canada. My hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Hoey), speaking the other day alleged that he believed that this would create a rate war between this new company and the monopoly in the United States, and that in his opinion the price of binder twine would be lower in western Canada for a number of years to come. He apparently was solicitous of the welfare of these capitalists who propose to come to Canada and establish this industry. They were quite willing to come to this country and risk some four or five million dollars in establishing such an industry. Their experts had come over here and looked over the field and were satisfied the industry would succeed if given a reasonable opportunity. I do not know on what ground my hon. friend sets up his opinion against that of these experienced men who had investigated the matter. I was rather surprised with his argument. I would have thought that a reduction in the price of twine to the farmers in western Canada would have appealed to him, and I was rather surprised that he set up his opinion against those of these experts who had looked over the field.

Does not my hon. friend see where his reasoning is leading him to? When the price is reduced and the hemp factory is in jeopardy we will have a demand for a protective tariff on binder twine coming to this country from the United States.

My hon. friend is setting up his opinion against that of the experts who looked over the ground and on whose opinion these capitalists were willing to risk four or five million dollars in this industry.

Anticipating protection.

There is a large field for this industry. In that respect it stands out from most other manufactures in this country. It will have a larger field in which to sell its product than its competitor in the United States. Now what will this do for Canada? Annually there is going out of this country from fifteen to sixteen million dollars for binder twine purchased at an exorbitantly high rate. Supposing this new industry did not lower the price of twine, this fifteen or sixteen million dollars would remain in Canada and help to build up industries in this country, and would give labour to thousands of our own people here. One lion, member immediately opposite me suggested the other day that we should give a bounty to the farmer who grew the hemp. The farmer who grows the hemp is in an entirely satisfactory condition, and this industry will mean giving him another markef right at his own door in which he can sell his products. If he can get more for the production of hemp than he can for the wheat he produces he will grow hemp; if he cannot get a price for his hemp equal to that he gets for his wheat he will not grow the hemp. So what we are really doing is to bring a market right to the fanner's own door.
Does not that same argument apply to the manufacturer of hemp -that if he could secure an adequate return he would produce?

The argument is this: The industry will be fighting against the monopoly in the United States, something my hon. friend is always prepared to fight. We have an abundance of cheap power that could be used in the manufacture of hemp :nto twine. The production of hemp will also assist in giving a diversified crop production on the farms of western Canada. The lands surrounding the city of Winnipeg are more or less fallowed and infested with weeds. The production of hemp will take the place of summer fallowing very largely and will be exceedingly profitable. By reason of the cheap power to be had by the manufacturing industry, by reason of the closeness of the market, by reason of the fact that the hemp manufactured will be produced on farming lands in western Canada and should be sold to the manufacturer at a cheaper price than it can be produced for on the higher priced lands of the United States, I believe this industry should succeed against the competition of the United States.
Bounty on Hemp
Why is the land surrounding Winnipeg polluted with weeds?
Because the farmers of western Canada have not been farming properly.

Does not my hon. friend
realize that flax is the worst possible thing to pollute the land?

My hon. friend represents a farming community but he has a most indefinite idea of what is produced upon a farm. Flax grows about two and a half feet high, and hemp eight or ten feet high; they are two different products altogether. In addition to what I have already said as to why we should encourage this industry there is the fact that employment will be given to the working people of western Canada. For that reason this legislation should have the support of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson), as it will have the effect of bringing to Winnipeg, or to the immediate environments of that city, a large enterprise which will take care of our working people there the year round. This proposition is a very desirable thing and should be supported not only by the members for Winnipeg, but by all the farming representatives from western Canada. I appeal to these hon. members to support a bill that will bring to the west a concern that should free them from the monopoly from which they are now suffering by reason of the International Harvester Company. I appeal to them to endorse a proposition which will create a market for a large acreage of hemp produced in the West, will assist in better farming methods, will keep millions and millions of dollars in this country, and will have the effect of freeing us from the domination of the United States. The farther we can advance along this line the better it will be. In the interest of some of our needs' in the future it may be very desirable that we should have industries in this country that will render us absolutely independent of the United States.
What about the binder twine manufacturing plant at Brantford?

That is a small plant
and does not, I believe, sell binder twine in western Canada at all. It is so insignificant that this great monopoly does not bother to fight it. But if a real competitor comes into the field then you may expect to see a war in connection with the sale of binder twine.

In reply to the very fair and reasonable proposition advanced by my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) I have this to say by way of argument:	We are to-day fighting a powerful monopoly. The manufacturers who propose to establish themselves in Canada contemplate investing a very large sum, probably some four or five million dollars. There is every prospect of success as I view the matter. Still, these men are going into a very hard fight, and I think it is only fair, in view of the benefit to be derived by our working people and the farmers of Canada as a whole, that they should receive some encouragement when they are undertaking to establish a new concern. It is not like making a new establishment in a line which has been in existence for some time; these men are venturing into a new field. And while the prospects look good, difficulties' may arise. If the promoters are willing to undertake the risk why should we not support them to a reasonable extent? The proposed bounty is not extravagant in its nature; in fact it is rather small. If I have any quarrel with the government, or with the minister, as I said before, it is that it is not proposed to give a bounty of such a character that assurance may be made doubly sure even from the very commencement. The bounty is small; it is not given for a lengthy period of time; it is on a sliding scale. Nevertheless the prospects for success are very bright. There is an opportunity here of establishing in western Canada an industry that will be indigenous to the country, that will stabilize conditions in the west, that will stimulate the farmer, that will provide employment for our people-in a word the proposition is one that should have the support of every western representative in the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I could hardly be expected to let the opportunity pass of making a few observations on the speech of the hon. member for North Winnipeg.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 3 o'clock.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
Are many of the
protected industries in this country not managed from the United States?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Not by any means, not
to the extent of an almost infinitesimal fraction. They are Canadian industries; American capital may be in them, but they are not part of a big American ring.

What about the Imperial
Oil Company?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Imperial Oil Company is, in the main, a Canadian company. How funny it is to see hon. gentlemen to your right rise! If such is the case, why do they not pursue their policy past binder twine and get us into such a shape that we shall have to give bounties to everything raised in this Dominion? I thought hon. gentlemen to my left would be slow to rise.
Is it true that we are buying binder twine cheaper than we did before the duty was removed and the wages were increased?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is not. Binder twine
is cheaper than it was four years ago; most things are; but it is much dearer than it was when w7e had the 12 per cent duty. I think it is dearer this year than it was last. As I say, out of this very school stands the prophet who declares that we are landed now in the grip of an American monopoly. He is not far from the fact; substantially he is within the truth, and out of this school stands one who says we are making in Canada 10 per cent of this big staple article of consumption by the people of this Dominion. Yes, I suppoit the legislation. I will support any such effort, however feeble, and I only hope at least a measure of success will result from it.

I am quite interested in the remarks of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen). Some of us have memories that reach back to those years when binder twine was 17 cents a pound, when we had a protective duty and dear labour.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: When was that?

That was when we
built a binder twine factory ourselves, and that is what they told us at the time it was 17 cents a pound, that these corporations he is talking about would force us down to a cost of 6 cents a pound and put us out of business. What happened at that time? Many men went into the business, and

if many of the farmers had put all their money into the business at that time, they would have made more money than they would in farming. The price of binder twine came down to 6 cents, and we succeeded in meeting that. My opinion is that no industiy starting in this country, in which it has an opportunity of making good, has a right to receive protection from other industries. Such industries have a right to stand on their own feet without any support. 1 am in entire support of the amendment. We have been carrying on too long this system of subsidizing infant industries in order to establish them, and I do not know how long it takes to get some of them established. We are apparently undertaking to carry more and more of these industries; this must stop some time, and my opinion is that we should stop it right now. We have been bonusing our railways; indeed in all our smaller towns-for instance, in my own town, we have been giving any amount of money to industries, and what has happened? The money has gone and the industry has gone. I am opposed to the continuation of granting bonuses; I am opposed to this particular one, and I will support the amendment.

I regret I cannot agree with the argument put forward by the hon. member for North AVinnipeg (Mr. Mu-Murray). I am aware that considerable pressure is being brought to bear from Winnipeg to have this particular matter go through; yet I cannot see how this case differs from hundreds of others that might be brought up from different parts of the country. I note, in the circular sent out by the Winnipeg Board of Trade one of the statements in favour of this matter is that this will be a source of revenue to the federal government by establishing an additional industry which will be subject to taxation. Possibly that is what has' appealed to the Minister of Finance. But I would submit that from the standpoint of good business, so far as the federal government is concerned, we may have to wait a very considerable time before any money secured in the form of taxation upon this industry will equal what will be expended in the proposed bonus. I think we can all agree with the member for North Winnipeg when he speaks about the fertility of the western plains, and the possibility of producing raw material in great abundance, there. I have very little doubt that is true. We can also agree, I think, that there is a splendid local market; undoubtedly the western fanners consume a great deal more of

Bounty on Hemp
these articles than are required elsewhere in this country. Still further, we all know that Winnipeg has cheap power and for that reason production should be carried on without a very heavy expenditure. But all these reasons would seem to show that this is a good business proposition, and if it is I cannot see why those who are interested in investing money should not come into the country without any other encouragement. We are told that if the prices are lowered the farmers will benefit, but I fail to see anything in the bill which will in any way ensure that the prices will be lowered, or that the alleged monopoly will be broken. We are also informed that this industry will be a very great benefit to the labouring classes. Well, if reasonable wages are paid and if there is steady work it may be advantageous to them. But there is no indication whatever that the rights of the labour people in this regard will be respected in this industry any more than they have been in any other industry.
We have been told that British capital is willing to come in and invest in this country. Let me remind hon. members that the statement was also made in the committee on Banking and Commerce that our banks have plenty of money to lend. If this is such a good thing and if the securities are going to be so sound there is no particular reason why British capital should not come in and the Canadian banks should not help to finance the institution while it is producing.
I would also suggest, that there are other alternatives which the government might consider. Some of us are very much interested in municipal or provincial enterprises. I cannot see why something of this kind should not be encouraged -in the same way as are those enterprises. Or why not, one might ask, bonus the farmers' co-operative societies that are already engaged in various types of productive industry, and if there is any benefit in the undertaking let those societies reap it? I might go so far as to suggest that there are some labour organizations which, if sufficiently bonused, could guarantee to carry on an industry of this kind. These are some of the alternatives to bonusing a group of British capitalists in the way proposed.
With regard to the amendment, I confess I am almost at a loss to know how to vote. As I am opposed to the principle of granting bonuses i't seems rather strange to support a motion granting in any form a privilege of this kind. On the other hand, until such time as we have greater control over our industry, and so long as private industry is the rule, I am willing to try experiments. It may be
in this instance a good thing to give this particular private industry an opportunity to develop. But more than that, I am rather anxious to test the bona tides of those who are putting forward this proposition, on the ground that it is in the general interest.
I submit that if this is indeed in the public welfare no group of men should hesitate to take the position that if the public advances money it should be in the shape of a loan which should have the first claim on the industry. For that reason I propose to support the amendment.

I am opposed to the granting of this bounty on the same ground that I oppose other bounties. No industry has been benefited, or has benefited this country, that has been established artificially. The history of bounties in Canada is just as sorry a spectacle, just as much a delusion and a fallacy as any other form of the old Nationa. Policy which was adopted by the Libera government from its predecessors in 1897 There has been a cry in this House against Americans benefiting by the exploitation of our natural resources. The bounties of 1897 and 1899, however, were given entirely to American promoters. The two companies established at Cape Breton and Sault Ste. Marie -were formed for the benefit of American promoters. In one case where money was given for the establishment of a plant, no steel was rolled until years afterwards. These two companies received many millions of Canadian money, the Sydney company, $6,500,000 and the Algoma company $2,600,000. What benefit did the Canadian people derive from those grants? Did we get steel any cheaper, or did our railway constructors get their rails at any lower rate? No. We paid from $11 to $13 a ton higher for our rails during that period than did any other country in the world; we could have secured them that much cheaper outside had we free trade. The bounties that were given to those two companies during those years more than paid the whole of the wages which the industries paid out to their employees. There was another bounty paid these mills in the years 1901 and 1902, but it was not until 1904 that one ingot was rolled in either of them. Why our government to-day is so eager to create monopolies by the granting of bounties and bonuses as well as tariff protection and the placing of embargoes on the export of raw material is more than I can understand. The steel bounties present one of the worst exhibitions of corruption and graft, and these bounties which the government now proposes but finds it hard to excuse, are likely to lead

Bounty on Hemp

to similar evils. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) I think is mistaken in some of the statements he has made. In 1898 the duty was taken off binder twine. We had an understanding about that time with the United States regarding manila from the Philippines, under which no undue import advantages were to be granted to their manufacturers as against ours. But I think the American manufacturers had an advantage of one-eighth of a cent per pound over ours, and we were reimbursing our manufacturers at the time to that extent, perhaps more. But during this period we never got twine in the West under 13, 14, 15 and 16 cents a pound. I am speaking of the early years of my settlement there. Before the war the farmers, under free trade, were getting twine as low as 7 and 8 cents a pound. I know this personally because I bought twine every season for over thirty years. I make the assertion that last year we could have bought twine at least 2 cents a pound cheaper had there been free trade in this commodity. Nominally twine is on the free list, but it is hedged about with such customs regulations that it can hardly be said to enter free. Last year an effort was made to bring the anti-dumping clause into force on an importation of twine by the United Farmers of Ontario, but it failed. That we are in the grip of an American monopoly in respect to this industry is simply a myth. If there is any industry languishing in this country it is not owing to free trade; the cause must be looked for elsewhere, and it is to be found in the fallacy of the National Policy, which advances the price of everything we have to buy and thus forces our cost of production out of line with that of other countries.
The best protection our manufacturers can have, and which this new industry in the West ought to cultivate, is a national sentiment. There is no doubt that our manufacturers have alienated this sentiment until to-day they find themselves more and more at a disadvantage under the tariff system. A truly national policy of "Canada for the Canadians, with fair play for all," is the best protection that our manufacturers can have. I say, let us be done with the whole system of tariff protection, bonuses and bounties.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the importance of the proposed legislation is my only justification for spending even five minutes in discussing it. I have a good deal of sympathy with my western friends who look with misgiving at anything resembling protection. I remember when this proposal was brought to my attention a year ago last Febru-

ary I loked at it askance because I realized that what we do as a matter of course provincially in the West is looked upon as straight protection when done by the federal authorities. In analyzing the activities of the provincial governments of the West, I naturally am led to review those of my own province of Saskatchewan, where we have given assistance to various industries, very much to their advantage. I have never taken the ground that no kind of assistance should be given industry for fear it might be called protection. It seems to me that this system is the least objectionable form of protection, because it is terminable, while the other kind that we dislike so much is apparently interminable. That is the great difference between the two.
Let me cite some of the things we have been doing in Saskatchewan. For instance, we have for many years given money at 3 per cent to our co-operative creamery, we have given it office accommodation, and we have been paying the freight on cream to the central plant. All this is in the nature of subsidies, bounties or assistance. But as a result we have the satisfaction to-day of having established one of the best co-operative creameries and cold storage plants anywhere in the Dominion. It having been developed into a successful undertaking, assistance has been withdrawn. Then again, we have two stockyard companies in the province to each of which we have granted a straight bonus of $25,000. My hon. friends from the West thought that was all right. How is it altogether wrong when we come down here and do exactly the same thing federally in connection with the hemp industry? A third instance is the substantial grant or bonus which the Saskatchewan government gave towards the building of telephone lines.

Is it not a fact that while the hon. minister was a member of the Saskatchewan government it passed a law prohibiting municipalities from granting bonuses or subsidies to induce industries to locate within their boundaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think that was in connection with the railways.
Also in connection with mills and such like.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There may be occasions when municipal bodies should not be subject to the temptation of competing with one another for the establishment of industries. But there is not such competition between provinces. The Saskatchewan govern-

Bounty on Hemp
ment also gave an initial grant at the time the co-operative elevator company was established, and since then, until quite recently at least, the trading account has been guaranteed by the provincial authorities all the way from 75 per cent down.
Were not these grants by the provincial government made to publicly owned utilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Certainly not, they are co-operative institutions owned by the people. The principle of this form of assistance has been recognized times without number and has never been condemned in Saskatchewan. I can understand my hon. friends' feelings in regard to this matter, because I know that the environment here is different to what we are accustomed to in Saskatchewan. Here we are suspected of sinister designs upon the Treasury when we suggest any form of assistance to industry, while the same thing could be done by the western provinces and be thought perfectly all right. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I have no hesitation in supporting the establishment and encouragement of this new industry. Why is it necessary to develop it? It has been developed up to the present to the extent of only ten per cent of our requirements. Our demands for binder twine alone, leaving out the other cordage commodities, have grown annually. We have grown this year to be the largest wheat export country in the world; we are the second largest wheat producing country. Surely, therefore, we should not any longer have to depend on a foreign country for our binder twine. When we first went into the West we had to make our own binding material out of straw. The proposal now is to make our own binder twine through the production of a commodity called hemp fibre, something that is indigenous to this country. Something that can be manufactured here. A band of Winnipeg men have put over $100,000 of their own capital into experiments connected with the growing of hemp. These experiments, carried on without aid for about fifteen years, were on two occasions almost on the point of success, but something always happened. It does seem to me, therefore, that if any industry deserves assistance of this kind it is the hemp industry. I recall the time during the war when there was a dearth of twine; our shipping was in jeopardy; the raw material had to come from the Philippines and in some instances from Mexico. It is true that the twine was being manufactured in the United States, but they had to depend very
largely upon foreign countries for their raw material, and even if those countries were friendly, the dangers of the sea were great. I have been impressed with the importance of the production of two things within our own country: One is fuel and the other is twine, and the production of both in Canada is possible. I see that the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is smiling now; he thinks I am advocating his fad, protection. But it is a terminable kind of protection. There are certain kinds of medicine, like strychnine, for example, which are beneficial if taken in small quantities, but which if taken in larger doses will knock you out. I propose that we take the medicinal dose, something that will do us good, not something that will kill us. The question has1 been asked, why does this industry not start up of its own volition.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I wonder if the
hon. member for Brome ever had anything to do with starting an industry, even as small as this.
I started my own law.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is quite a
different proposition; there are certain advantages there that do away with the need for any kind of assistance. Now, at the annual meetings of the Dairy Association in Saskatchewan I used to warn the farmers that as soon as their industry began to be self-sustaining, as soon as it could stand on its own feet, their assistance would be lessened or withdrawn. I used to say at Saskatoon: We are going to take a certain amount of assistance off this year; we are going to stop paying the express to the central creameries, and next year we are going to stop assisting you in the matter of office staff and office accommodation." It was all right so long as they knew that these curtailments were coming; and it always brought them to time when I would say to them: "You do not want to be in the same category as the eastern manufacturer, wanting this assistance forever." When I would say that they would immediately come across and agree to let the assistance drop. That is what we propose here. We have had two indications this year that these bounties are terminable. They may come along and ask that the bounty be further extended, but surely we can have backbone enough to say nay to them. Take the question of the flax bounty. If I were to give my candid opinion, I think we should have extended that bounty for 'another year, but
Bounty on Hemp

rather than put ourselves in the position of being led on by this bounty proposition, we terminated the flax bounty which was being paid to the institution at Guelph. So with the bounty on oil; that has been adjusted so that it will disappear, I think, at the end of another year. We must either assist this hemp industry in some legitimate way, in some way that we can see the end of, or *we shall have to go on forever buying our twine from foreign countries. Which do we prefer?
I remember the time when we could take out almost in one car the whole binder twine requirements of Saskatchewan, but since that time the requirement has never ceased to grow, and I am confident that it will keep on growing larger and larger as the country becomes1 settled. The question is, are we to continue buying our binder twine from another country and running the chance of going without it at some critical time, or are we to develop a Commodity that can be produced right in Canada? For many years I found that the soil on my own farm was so rich that it would not grow wheat to maturity in time to escape the frost. In many districts in northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba it is not good business to grow wheat, but it may be an exceedingly profitable business to grow hemp. I am satisfied that hemp can be produced in northern Alberta as well as in the southern part of the province by irrigation; that flax seed and flax fibre can also be successfully produced in those districts, and that this industry may ultimately be developed in Manitoba and in the entire West-right to the Pacific, if you like. When I became interested in this product last year I gave instructions to the Director of Experimental Farms to try out the growing of hemp in all the experimental farms, and it was found that it could be grown in every province. I say there is no reason why, when this industry gets well established, it cannot be extended all over Canada. When I had the painful opportunity of reading the speech of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) on this question, he made what seemed to me to be the strongest possible argument for this bounty: he suggested that the price of International twine would be so cut that the new institution would be put out of business. Well, if no assistance were given, that is what would happen, and that is exactly the justification for the assistance. In the early days of an enterprise like this, when the overhead is large and the turnover is small, the cost per pound must be excessive, and if you are

going to get into competition with an old-established institution like the International Harvester Company, they can cut their price by two or three cents and beat you out. Under those circumstances, unless a business were enormously strong it would soon have to close its doors. That is not a dream; that is not protectionist theory; it is something that anybody can realize would happen if you start something that comes into competition with an institution that has been long established and has attained full growth. I do not think I can give my hon. friends any better illustration than this: If you take an immature farm animal-a calf, a pig, or a foal -and put it in the same pen with a full grown animal and leave it to rustle for itself, how do you think it will flourish? With these illustrations I will sit down as the weather is getting rather warm.

I should like to make one
correction as the minister has created a false impression. Where help has been given to an industry in Saskatchewan it has always been a public owned utility organized to help the people help themselves. It is this creating monopolies that will in the end fleece the people that we object to.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I do not understand my hon. friend. In the little telephone companies that were organized it was the individuals w}io benefited. It was not a giant monopoly, and this is not a giant monopoly. We are simply encouraging new capital to come to Canada to engage in a new industry that my hon. friend and thousands of others require in this country.

It is not to be publicly
owned.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I prefer making
my own product. If we are going to buy everything abroad we shall soon not be able to buy what we want at home.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is nothing that so cheers the heart of the old battle-scarred veteran as the sight of a young, vigorous and belligerent recruit coming to his aid. I welcome the adhesion even of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). I do not need any memory at all to recall the part the hon. gentleman played when in the ranks of the foe. There dins in my ears even now the battle cry against special privilege that rang through the Progressive press and from Farmer and Progressive and Liberal platforms in western Canada. Special privilege was the curse of the nation, special privilege was

Bounty on Hemp
something against which every righteous man, every honest man, strikes his blow. And in that battle right in the ranks, yes, in the very front, stood the hon. Minister of Agriculture, and if he did not carry the flag or .ride a horse he at least beat the drum. But protection now is all right so long as it is mild. He finds that he cannot enter the lists now against special privilege because it is borne in upon him that all t'he while he was crying out himself and his newspapers crying behind him, we were giving special privilege ourselves, he says. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We were continually being met by a free trade crusade engineered partly by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). There was only a certain amount that we were able to do. We did very well; and, moreover, through most of that time war conditions prevailed. Under those war conditions, it was impossible to recreate industries of that character in this country. I do not know what the hon. member means. Does he mean to chastise us because we kept the tariff averaging as low as we did? He is rather late in the day in commencing that course. I do not know but that on more articles than one we did keep the tariff lower than was for the ultimate benefit of the country. If I were to plead guilty to any indictment, that would be the one that I would plead guilty to, but I do not believe that plea will give much encouragement to hon. gentlemen opposite or to hon. gentlemen to my left.
The hon. member (Mr. Milne) said that there was a greater difference between the 1913 price and the 1922 price on binder twine than on most other things, although there were some exceptions. Let us take freights, for instance. I think transportation charges have considerably more than

doubled in the period from 1899 to the present time. Wages have probably tripled. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) made some references to conditions obtaining in Saskatchewan, but I contend that there is no analogy between that and this kind of a bonus to an industry. I do not know that the Saskatchewan government at any time bonused any private industry. It is true that the telephone system in Saskatchewan is a joint stock company, but it is owned purely by the individual owners and users of the line.

We m'ght just as well say that it is a serious state of affairs that we do not raise one per cent of the bananas used in this country. Sisal hemp and manila are not indigenous to this country, and I am very doubtful whether hemp will ever be successfully manufactured into binder twine in Canada. I do not, however, think there is in this section of the House any hon. member who would not give his best wishes to this industry, and I do not think anyone in western Canada and probably in eastern Canada who does not hope that the industry will be successful. But coupled with that, there is always this fear, that if it be successful, then we shall have an annual pilgrimage to this House to demand a duty on binder twine, and the protective argument will be put up as a reason why we should have that duty. In the end, probably this will cost the farmers of the West a good deal more than they make on the hemp.

speechtext: Without cutting into the interesting discussion between the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) and hon. gentlemen to his left, I should like to call attention to a fallacy which ran through the whole argument of the leader of the Opposition with regard to the figures on binder twine. He appears to have assumed that on the Liberal side it was claimed that the tariff governs the price. Nobody ever proposed such a foolish thing as that. Whatever the price of binder twine was from time to time, it was by reason, not of the tariff, but of the cost of raw materials, transportation, labour. All those elements enter into the price of binder twine. It is absolutely safe to make this remark: Whether the price was low or high in any of those years, whatever it was, it would have been so much higher if the old duty of 12J per cent had remained.

I feel compelled to vote against both the amendment and the resolution, and in doing so I want to give a word of explanation. I voted before lunch for the bounty on copper, and that action of mine led me into a difficult situation amongst my friends on this side of the House, because they harked back to the action I took on oleomargarine the other day. They seem to have some difficulty in following the tortuous course of my actions. I do not want to enter very deeply into this discussion, except to state once more my underlying political philosophy. I think, having stated it, my course will explain itself. I am not here as a defender of any economic theory, because I realize that the people, at least my constituents, cannot live on theories. They are ordinary men and women of flesh and blood, and they have not yet acquired the habit of living under the air-bell of any economic theory. My actions are all in relationship to that view, and I want to say that if the rural dwellers of Canada do not see this yet, they are destined to see it, namely that the following of any theory, no matter how sacred it is as a theory, will not get them anywhere. It has not got them anywhere in the last

fifty years and, as I gauge the political situation at the present time, it will not get them anywhere in the next fifty. There must be a change in the attitude of mind of the rural dweller of Canada if his livelihood is to be protected, if his standard of living is to be maintained in some reasonable comparison with that of the city dweller. The rural dweller of Canada for a great many years has followed the star of free trade and at last he has fallen into the pit of political impotence; and he is destined to abide there if he cannot become practical in his political allegiance. I spoke as I did on the oleomargarine question rather out of sympathy with the dairy farmer than for any other reason, and I made the mistake of using the language of irony. But realizing the danger of that practice I warned the House in the course of my speech that I was speaking ironically.
I know, of course, that such language is al* ways double-edged, but notwithstanding my warning I found, after I had concluded my speech that I had wounded my friends more than my enemies. From that point of view I had a great deal of sympathy with his position, although I am not a dairy farmer myself, nor a representative of dairy farmers.

hemp, and produce them equally well. With regard to copper and my vote on that question I frankly own that I made concessions to the isolated community to the north of my constituency, a community that has practically no representation in this House because it is in the minority and has no influence, to speak of, on the representation in parliament. I make that concession frankly to the people on the north side of the Nelson constituency, not with any idea that it will serve my own purposes, because I do not believe for a moment that it will. This matter of bounties contains no element of principle for me. A bounty, as I look at it, should be allowed or disallowed according to its practical bearing on the interests of the country as a 'whole. I am not admitting for a moment that there is any principle herein contained, and I certainly do declare that so far as my conscience is concerned my action is perfectly clear and straightforward.
With regard to hemp, on which I am reversing my vote, let me state the situation. My constituency, on its south side, is well adapted to the growing of hemp, but the farmers there, although their land will grow this product, do not look upon it as a practical proposition, so far at least as they are concerned. - The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) states that the north of Manitoba is not adapted to wheat growing. I want to correct him in. that regard: There is no part of the west of Canada that can grow wheat to compete with that produced in the Swan River valley, comprising the south part of my constituency, and I make no exception whatsoever. It is recognized to be the best wheat growing section in the whole of the West, and there is no such thing as a crop failure in my constituency. For that reason the farmers are not interested i:i hemp. They believe that hemp producing would involve them in additional work in the fall of the year when attention to their crops is all-important. Moreover, they do not believe that the length of the season in the fall is sufficient for the attention which is required in the proper curing of good hemp. This is not my own opinion, for my own opinion is not concerned; I have it on the authority of a very representative body of farmers in my constituency. They do not think that there is any advantage in this bounty on hemp; if there were, I believe they would possibly be in favour of it. I know from experience that the farmer of Canada is not a theorist; he is not wedded to any theory. And why should he be?

Too long has he been misled by theoretical propositions; he has followed that will-of-the-wisp for all these years and has got nothing thereby. He has been led into the never-ending controversy on the	respective
merits of protection and free trade, which question has blinded him to his own interest, so that he has come out the loser. And so far as I can see he will continue to lose. I think I am representing the attitude of the farmer of western Canada when I say that he has no interest in any theory as such; I cannot conceive his being so foolish as to have any such interest. I believe he is becoming sufficiently enlightened	on	theeconomic and political questions	of	thiscountry and is no longer to be fooled by mere theories. The situation of the farmer is rather suggestive of the method used in the capturing of a gamecock. They bring along a gamecock in capitivity and place it near the free bird. Presently the two become so absorbed in their mutual attentions that the owner of the captive comes along and catches them both. That is typical, I think, of the case of the Canadian farmer. The political parties have succeeded	in	ensnaring the farmer in the controversy between protection and free trade, and in the process the rural dweller has been deceived and has got nothing in the result. One would think that having been so badly left behind he would have learned wisdom; but the occurrences of the last few days show that the farmer of Canada has not learned wisdom yet. He has still the desire to pursue the rut which leads towards no profitable goal. In making this explanation, I hope that my hon. friends will not misunderstand me when I indulge in the somewhat dangerous practice of using a two-edged phrase, because I have no other reason for being here than to help our rural men and women receive a better proportion of the good things of life that are being produced in this wonderfully wealthy Dominion.

I believe the government
