At the risk of offending those who wish to get out of this "torrid" chamber I shall venture to make a few remarks. We have had a very interesting exposition of political philosophy from my hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Bird). I take issue with him mildly in regard to the application of what I consider to be a very sound principle. When he enunciates the welfare of the nation as' the only principle worth considering in deciding between protection and free trade, I think he is on safe ground. I would suggest that if we are convinced that one policy is better than the other, always bearing in mind the common welfare, then he and I are perfectly agreed. I use the very same principle as a test of either protection or free trade, and from a fairly close study of the matter leaving aside for the time being considerations of political economy, the general policy of free trade works out very much more to the advantage of any nation adopting it than does the policy of protection. If we are going to divide ourselves into a number of classes or communities seeking something for ourselves aS such, I do not know what we are coming to. Certainly I very much question the advisability of taking this position.
I regret that the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) is not in his seat. I think he is really too shrewd to believe half of what he said this afternoon. For instance, in reference to his quotation of the prices of binder twine, it must be obvious to him, as was partially pointed out by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), that there are many other considerations entering into the determination of price. I would add to those already enumerated by the minister that the price index, or the general price level, has to be kept in mind in any comparison of figures.
As for the competition between towns, which was referred to by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, I agree with him that it is just as objectionable and just as unjustifiable as the competition between nations.
I think we are prepared to admit that generally speaking such competition between communities is reprehensible. If so, I submit it calls for just as strong condemnation when indulged in between nations'.

I think the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) ought to remember the danger of taking habit-forming drugs. In the actual working out of this policy of giving bounties, subsidies or tariff protection, we nearly always find that after we take the drug for a few years we acquire the habit, and it is almost impossible to break it off.
I believe the right hon. leader of the Opposition left a wrong impression on the Hous-e with regard to the binder twine industry. I happen to live near the Brantford binder twine factory-one of the few survivors of the 'nineties. It has been alleged that the abolition of the protective tariff on binder twine brought about a number of bankruptcies and general disaster to those engaged in the industry. I regret that I have not the detailed analysis of the situation which was made two years ago by, I think, the Toronto Star, but, speaking from memory, the actual statistics as to production will not bear out the statement made by the leader of the Opposition. If my recollection serves me, the relative production has not decreased in Canada. And the factory at Brantford has gone ahead by leaps and bounds. The management have had difficulty in keeping up with the demand for their products. It has been impossible to get a sufficient amount of capital in the industry to expand fast enough to meet the growing demand, and this in spite of the fact that they were face to face with competition from the larger binder twine industries in the States. A number of our Canadian binder twine concerns which went to pieces at the time referred to were in the promotion stage. If the right hon. leader of the Opposition looks into the statistics carefully, I think he will find that his statement is not correct, and that to speak of the binder twine industry as having been brought to an emaciated, gasping condition by the abolition of the duty in 1898 is very far from the fact.
One more thought I should like to present to him and to the House, particularly to some hon. members opposite -who have perhaps some lingering belief in the gospel-shall I say?-of freer trade. If industry, speaking generally, could be stimulated by this method which we are so prone to adopt at the present time, which seems very plausible and which I notice commends itself to men like the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. McMurray) and a number of his associates, including the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell),-if it could be stimulated in this way, then surely we would have had happier results for following this policy. I submit that a careful examination of the
facts will show that if you stimulate one industry it can only be at the expense of some other industry, that where you build up one you tear down another,. and on the average the whole result is negative rather than positive. I submit as a general principle in that connection that a mistaken ptiblio polioy based on an economic fallacy must lead to disaster. As for me I am quite prepared to stand-

Is it not a fact that the Brantford factory of which my hon. friend speaks so approvingly received its start under a system of protection and that when the tariff wall went doivn it flourished? The very :i lustration he gives contradicts his own argument.
No, far from it. If I remember rightly this factory was built before the abolition of the duty in 1897.

That is what I say.
_ Mr. GOOD: It is quite true it was built before that time, but it had a very precarious existence for some years and it was on the point of bankruptcy when the present manager took over the job. I had it from frequent conversations with him that the success of that industry has been almost wholly, if not entirely due to careful management. He has stated on more occasions than one, I think even publicly, that he and his associates have no desire for any tariff protection. The success of that factory has been marked since the abolition of the duty; prior to that time they were getting along in a very limping way. These are the facts. I simply wanted to impress this upon the committee-and I am sorry the right hon. leader of the Opposition is not here-that we have tried out this policy in Canada and the results have been disastrous. We ought therefore to pause and examine the course we have taken. Having regard to the results that have been secured from this fiscal policy, we ought to be quite certain as to the basic principles involved before we trust our future to it.

Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance moved the second reading of Bill No. 242, to amend the Export Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Governor in Council may by regulation prohibit export of pulpwood.

Before this clause is
carried I wish to direct a few observations to the House. I think it was the celebrated Doctor Johnson who made the following reply when asked by his landlady as to the condition in which certain food came before him: "Madam, this meat was ill-killed, ill-dressed, ill-cooked and ill-served." Apparently it was undesirable from all points of view. And, with all respect for those who are responsible for this legislation, I have the same feeling concerning it. This is not the first time that legislation of this sort has been brought before the House during the last few years. The Protectionist and Unionist government in 1920 brought in a similar though a wider measure before the House. In the session of 1920 Sir Robert Borden moved:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Customs Act, and to provide that the Governor in Council may from time to time make regulations for or relating to the exportation of any article, commodity or material which is produced or manufactured in Canada, and which is, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, necessary or desirable for the use or consumption of the Canadian people, or for the encouragement, maintenance or preservation of any trade, industry, business or occupation, and may by such regulations order and direct that any such article, commodity or material shall be exported only under license issued by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue, or by an officer appointed upon the minister's recommendation for that purpose.
I will not read the whole resolution, but I would direct the attention of the House to what I consider very sound observations made
at that time by the now Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Bureau). After referring to this legislation he spoke as follows:
For my part, I would like to know of some concrete cases in connection with which legislation of this kind becomes necessary in time of peace and under ordinary conditions. We complain that we have a large debt; that our currency is at a discount; that the balance of trade is against us. Now we are going to place in the hands of the government the power to restrict exports of any kind of commodity. Whatever the reason may be, I do not think that there is any emergency to call for action of that kind. Unless the special committee submit a report on the matter which changes my mind, I shall be absolutely and entirely opposed to vesting such power in the Governor in Council.
I addressed the House on the same occasion and spoke as follows:
This proposed legislation is to my mind so vicious that I wish to have an opportunity given on the introduction of the resolution of speaking to it. It would be very well for the country to be fully advised as to what the government purpose doing. I would have thought that the Canadian nation was thoroughly sick of the government endeavouring to control industry, and it is surely bad enough to have a protectionist government in power with the right to control imports into the country, but it would be worse to have them control exports from the country.
It was on that basis that I opposed the resolution at that time. However, the resolution was referred to a special committee. That committee went into the matter. Subsequently Sir Robert Borden begged leave to withdraw the resolution and it was withdrawn on the 30th June, 1920. I commend
5 p.m. the action of Sir Robert Borden in that connection to the present administration.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in some remarks directed to this quarter of the chamber some time ago, referred to the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) having raised a little altar of his own. I admit the fact. But I would remind him that at least the fires of that altar are not fed by splinters from a broken platform. I would draw his attention to the fact that when he made those observations he stated that he was in favour of the principle of free trade, but in order to be on a level with the United States, who had placed high duties against our goods we had to place high duties against them. I will not enter into an argument as to either the soundness of the economics or the soundness of the logic contained in that statement, but I would direct the Prime Minister's attention to the fact that the United States have no duties, as far as I am aware, against exports from that country of pulpwood or any other commodity: that their desire is to further advance their foreign trade and not
Export Act-Pulpwood

to restrict it. The Golden Rule was said by Mr. Roosevelt to be not only good morality but sound politics; I think it is a particularly wise rule to follow when the other party is very much stronger and more powerful than yourself. " Do as you would be done by." This is more especially desirable when the other party is ten times more powerful than yourself. If we are to prohibit the export of pulpwood from this country what are we doing? We are inviting reprisals. I do not know whether they will come or not but we are certainly inviting them. What would the situation be supposing the United States restricted the export of hardwood from that country? What would the furniture manufacturers in western Ontario do to replace their raw , material, the hardwood that is brought in from the United States? They would certainly suffer, and with them the Canadian people. How long could our cotton mills proceed to carry on their business if there was an export duty placed on cotton, or its export into Canada were restricted? They could not carry on very long.
What about coal?

* An hon. member asks "What about coal?" I was just going to speak of coal. The whole of central Canada is warmed in winter, generally speaking, by anthracite coal brought from the United States, and we who live in central Canada would not contemplate with any equanimity our source of supply being interfered with. Indeed, suppose the United States in reprisal adopted an embargo against degrees from American universities? What would happen in that connection, or even if invitations to address Rotarian clubs in that country were prohibited?
What influence has been at work upon the .government to bring them to this frame of mind? The senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) told us that the Liberal party had a frame of mind looking towards free trade. Restriction of exports is not an evidence of a frame of mind reflecting free trade. What has deflected the Liberal party from its frame of mind, according to the senior member for Halifax? Is it those gentlemen in the country whose raw material is pulpwood and who wish to be in a position to buy pulpwood cheaper because there will be fewer buyers in the market? If it is those gentlemen who think their interest will be advanced by such a restriction, they are very short-sighted and they are making a great mistake. For, what are they likely to run into? If hon. gentlemen will turn up the United States statutes, cumu-

lative supplement of 1923, they will see on page 347 a paragraph in the American tariff which reads:
Par. 1301. Printing paper, not specially provided for one-fourth of one cent per pound and 10 per centum ad valorem: Provided, that if any country, dependency, province, or other subdivision of government shall forbid or restrict in any way the exportation of (whether by law, order, regulation, contractual relation, or otherwise, directly or indirectly), or impose any export duty, export license fee, or other export charge of any kind whatsoever (whether in the form of additional charge or License fee or otherwise) upon printing paper, wood pulp, or wood for use in the manufacture of wood pulp, the President may enter into negotiations with such country, dependency, province, or other subdivision of government to secure the removal of such prohibition, restriction, export duty, or other export charge, and if it is not removed he may, by proclamation, declare such failure of negotiations, setting forth the facts. Thereupon, and until such prohibition, restriction, export duty, or other export charge is removed, there shall be imposed upon printing paper provided for in this paragraph, when imported either directly or indirectly from such country, dependency, province, or other subdivision of government, an additional duty of 10 per centum ad valorem and in addition thereto an amount equal to the highest export duty or other export charge imposed by such country, dependency, province, or other subdivision of government, upon either an equal amount of printing paper or an amount of wood pulp or wood for use in the manufacture of wood pulp necessary to manufacture such printing paper.
That is the situation in which this country may find itself if it attempts to restrict. Surely we have had long enough in this country restriction of the right of purchase; but the modern restrictionist wishes to restrict us in the right to sell, and that may land the country in this undesirable position, that our foreign trade in regard to pulpwood may be considerably prejudiced. I think also I might call the attention of the government to this fact, that the passing or bringing into force of such legislation as this, is to ill requite the action of the American people as regards the supply of anthracite coal which we have noticed for the last few years. In this part of Canada we have had for one or two winters back a scarcity of anthracite coal, and we have found that the United States, although they were themselves suffering from a shortage, saw that Canada got its fair proportion. This is a very poor requital for their generosity in that regard.
What is the real theory, what. is the real principle that one should follow in this connection as in other matters of this kind? I take it that after a Canadian citizen has grown a bushel of wheat, or manufactured a cheese, or cut a log, or cut a cord of pulpwood, he should have the right to exchange that for the very best value he can obtain, either inside or outside of this country. I see no other proper theory or principle to follow.

Export Act-Pulp wood
And this legislation, if applied, is directly contrary to that. This constitutes a bad precedent, but before I touch on the question of this precedent, let me state how this will affect people in my riding.
I do not often make appeals based on how a matter will affect people in my riding. I do not consider myself purely a mere delegate to think simply of the interests of my constituents, but I consider myself as a representative of the whole people, although I am elected from a certain constituency. In this ease I believe the interest of my constituency marches on all fours with the interest of the whole country. Under this legislation a farmer in my riding who wishes to sell a certain quantity of pulpwood, let us say to Richford, Vermont, or to an American paper mill, somewhere to the south, will find himself hampered. He will not be able to get the price that he otherwise would obtain for it. That is unjust; it is not right; it is not consistent with the principles which we would have supposed would animate a party calling itself a Liberal party. It is a bad precedent. If it is right to do this, if it is right, in the interest, let us suppose, of the newsprint manufacturers to limit the right of sale of pulpwood to producers, then it is right, in the interest of the millers, to limit the right of export of the grain producers, the wheat producers. There is no limit to the application of this principle, once it is admitted. It is a most unwholesome precedent.
I had the honour to be a member of the last parliament, and I took some part in the consideration of public questions which came before that parliament and in the debates which w'e held. One of the strongest arguments which we used against the continuance in power of the distinguished leader of the Opposition and the group which surrounded him, was that they were too fond of tryina to govern this country by orders in council. We stated that time and time again in the House, and the matter went pretty widely throughout the country. This was one of the reasons, one of the concomitant reasons which led to his defeat. Now what do we find? We find that this unwholesome practice of government by order in council is introduced in connection with this legislation; that some fine morning three months from now, if this legislation passes, the farmers may find that an order in council has been passed in Ottawa restricting their right to sell certain of their wood products to the United States.
When Clovis, one of the first of the Frankish kings was baptized into the church of the day, St. Remi said to him: "Courbe la tete, fier Sicambre, adore ce que tu as brule, brule
ce que tu as adore." "Burn what thou hast adored and adore what thou hast burned." I do not know who is the St. Remi who has given this advice to the present administration but I do know that in this regard the present administration is doing precisely what St. Remi advised Clovis he should do.
I may bring my remarks to a close. I do not wish to detain the committee, but I know that I am on sound Liberal ground in making the protest that I do. I cannot, however, fail to think that a picture which I see before my mind is a somewhat true picture. I see the present administration as a ship, the Prime Minister as its captain, the Minister of Finance as its first mate, and the Minister of Justice as its second mate. In accordance, it seems to me, with orders issued by the second mate, the first mate has thrown overboard the compass. It had become somewhat depolarized before it was confided to the deep. The chart has followed. The starboard watch-for "starboard" means the "steer-board," the side which controls the ship-* watch the chart going down into the ocean, with their faces wreathed in smiles. The port watch do not feel quite so happy. They wonder whether it is worth while launching the life boat in order to recover the chari before it sinks into the ocean. While they are contemplating and waiting, the chart goes down, down, down! No chart, no compass! The ship without a course, without a compass, without a chart, is driven on by this wave of protectionist feeling and wind of protectionist sentiment, until it will, I am sorry to say, inevitably be shipwrecked on the rock of a hostile and, I am afraid, justly exas perated public opinion.

I wish to make just two or three remarks at this stage, since I intend to move the six months' hoist on the third reading of the bill. I simply wish to point out to the committee and to hon. members representing certain rural constituencies, that the bill as it is now submitted to the House purports to prohibit the exportation of pulpwood from all lands, the bill to be put into force by order in council at any time after publication of the regulations for four consecutive weeks in the Canada Gazette. What does this mean? It is true it has been intimated to the House by the Minister of Finance, and I think by some other speakers, that the bill will not have for effect the prohibition of the exportation of pulpwood cut from lands belonging to farmers. We have the word of the Minister of Finance to that effect and I am quite willing to take it; I believe he will stand by that promise.
Export Act-Pulpwood

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that absolutely. What I pointed out was that suggestions of that character had been offered and would be considered; but I gave no decision on the point.
That only makes my argument stronger.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps.

I am glad that the minister has made that statement. At any rate, the government promises to consider the question as to whether or not the exportation of pulp-wood to the United States from 'lands belonging to farmers will be prohibited. I think that so long as the present government remains in power it is highly improbable that it would go the extreme lengths mentioned in the bill. But what guarantee is there that the party led by my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) may not some day come into power-stranger things have happened, strange things happened yesterday-and do just what the bill proposes? If I understand rightly the views of the right hon. gentleman and those of his followers, they are pledged to prohibit absolutely and totally the exportation of pulpwood from all freehold lands in the Dominion. In what position would my hon. friends be placed who come from the border counties, such as Brome, and a number of constituencies in Quebec and Ontario where the pioneer settlers in what I might call the backwoods are obliged, in order to cultivate their lands and to eke out their existence while discharging their homestead obligations, to sell pulpwood? In what position would they find themselves if after four weeks' notice they were told that they might no longer export wood to the United States? They would find that the price of pulpwood had so diminished that it would not pay them to take it off their land. I simply warn my colleagues on both sides of the House of the results that will attend this legislation, and I sincerely hope that while there is yet time the government may decide to postpone further consideration of the bill until the commission which it proposes to appoint shall have made a full report on the matter.

Last year, along with other members of the House, I got frequent communications from a Mr. Barnjum, who was interested in the preservation of our forest resources. I think we were all very much impressed with the representations made by him in that connection; we were impressed with
 *
the tremendous importance of preserving our forest resources against fire and damage by insects, and so on. Those communications have continued during this year, and I have noticed one rather singular and to me significant fact in connection with the very excellent representations regarding the preservation of our forest resources, namely this, that those representations usually wound up with the recommendation that, as our supply of pulpwood was rapidly being exhausted, we should prohibit its export. I have looked into these representations and I want to say briefly that so far as I can see the parties who were-I would not say, using Mr. Barnjum, although the circumstances would seem to suggest that idea-at all events, those who were interested in the prohibition of the exportation of our pulpwood apparently wanted to prevent competition from the other side. The statement was made, for instance, that we should build up the pulp industry on the north side of the St. Lawrence rather than on the south side. Well, I submit that it does not make any difference to the demands on our pulpwood whether the pulp mill is on one side of the river or the other; you will use the same amount of pulpwood. I am of the opinion, from my careful reading of the representations and the recommendation to which I have referred, that the very necessary precautions that we ought to take to preserve our forest resources have been used as a cloak for an attempt to carry out a policy intended to benefit a few pulp men in Canada by protecting them against competition for the purchase of pulpwood from the other side. That is the way I regard the situation, and I cannot but feel that the whole thing in that respect bears a sinister aspect. Let me say that I am absolutely in sympathy with every possible effort that either this government or the provincial governments may make to protect and increase our forest resources. But I consider that the proposition to prohibit the exportation of pulpwood has no connection whatsoever therewith, and that the bill now before the committee giving this power to the Governor in Council is a very dangerous and objectionable measure.

speechtext: Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the third reading of Bill No. 234, respecting the construction of Canadian National Railway Lines.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to move an amendment to this motion and to refer but very briefly indeed to the debate of yesterday on the same subject. It will be remembered that I endeavoured to show the House yesterday that heretofore all the moneys required for railway construction, capital investment, deficits, all purposes connected with our railways, were, under the practice that had prevailed, included in the estimates and consequently the country was informed each year as to just what the commitments of the nation were with respect to our railways. I endeavoured to show that in that way parliament had retained control over the annual expenditure. These were the principles that were embodied in the practice. It will be recalled that exception was taken to my statement at the time by the Minister of Finance, who stated that the estimates merely provided for deficits for such moneys as were needed for administration and operation. A somewhat sharp difference of opinion arose. I adhered to my view. Well, it is scarcely necessary to say that the facts bear me out. But I go further. The law of the land provides that; the law of the land compels it, nor did the late government ever attempt anything else. The Canadian National Railway Act in section 16 reads as follows-I shall not read it all:
Expenses shall be paid out of the receipts and revenues. Deficits sha/11 be payable out of Consolidated Revenue Fund. ,
But here is the precaution:
In the event of a deficit occurring at any time during any fiscal year the amount of such deficit shall from time to time be payable by the Minister of Finance out oS any unappropriated moneys in the Con-
C.N.R.-Construction

solidated Revenue Fund of Canada, the amounts paid by the minister under this section to be included in the Estimates submitted to parliament at its first session following the close of such fiscal year; and in the event of a surplus existing at the close of any fiscal year such surplus shall be paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Now as to moneys to provide for capital investment, these are covered by section 23, which reads as follows:
With the approval of the Governor in Council-
This is the section that was in question with the now celebrated Hotel Scribe:
With the approval of the Governor in Council. . . sanctioned by the Minister of Railways and Canals, the company may from time to time construct and operate rail was' lines-
Exactly the wording of the present legislation.
-branches and extensions, or railway facilities or properties of any description in respect to the conduction whereof respectively, parliament may hereafter authorise the necessary expenditure, or the guarantee of an issue of the company's securities. A copy of any plan and profile made in respect of any completed railway shall be deposited with the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.
And pursuant to those laws of this parliament every dollar for the purposes of the railway, whether to be raised by guarantee or advances in cash, was included in the estimates. The House will scarcely be surprised to learn that when the bill was going through in connection with the loans to the companies, although nothing else was ever intended but that the money should be each year voted by parliament, hon. gentlemen opposite rose and insisted that a clause go in compelling the submission to parliament. That submission was immediately adhered to and a clause put in, and these hon. gentlemen now, and chiefly the Prime Minister, who at page 1539 of the Hansard of 1919 railed in derision at the government for not having a clause in to provide that each year the money should be submitted in the estimates, and who declared that without it parliament would lose all its control, and who as a consequence had the clause put in, now comes to parliament with a bill and apparently is going to get the quiescent approval of this House to provide that the government does not need to put in the estimates any more the moneys advanced to the National Railways for construction purposes. This is of course a change of front, but a change of front is the invariable rule, in fact it is about the >
only consistent thing about the government-a change of front on every piece of legislation and policy. I for my part desire to do what we did, and did willingly, in 1919. I desire to provide for the retention by parliament of its control

year by year of the amount of the people's money that is going out that year, and I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens):
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to Committee of the Whole with instructions to amend same so as to provide that the money or guarantees of money required for the purposes of the said bill must for each year appear in the estimates and be voted by parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that every appropriation for the public service and every obligation assumed in the name of the government of Canada shall be subject to a direct vote of the House of Commons is a principle to which we can all subscribe. But I do not agree with my hon. friend in his insistence that all items should appear in the estimates. He said, using a quotation a moment ago, that it was essential that the House should know year by year the outgo for the year. Now there is nothing in the law which my hon. friend has quoted to show that it is essential that all items shall be voted in the estimates. The essence of the law is that the moneys shall be voted by parliament, an<^ parliament is now being asked to vote the moneys for this particular purpose. Again and again in the course of the discussion yesterday the hon. gentleman said that we were asking for a blank cheque. He magnified the situation as to how the Minister of Railways might enlarge or diminish or lengthen the mileage of the railways. In that case the essence is that a railway has to be constructed from A to B. That is the vital question. But if the mileage estimated by the engineers is sixty-two miles, and it turns out to be sixty-one or sixty-three miles, there is no vital error if you take the money that is appropriated and apply it to that purpose. There is no blank cheque so long as you state your sum and state the purpose for which it is to be voted. A railroad from A to B shall be constructed, and the sum is stated and you cannot go beyond that. Again I say, the vital question is not that the item shall appear in the estimates, but that the money shall be appropriated by a vote of parliament.
I called the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that the railway subsidies involving millions of dollars have always been voted in a separate bill. He said no, and later qualified that and said perhaps-he was not sure. I am sure that these railway subsidies, and they are quite akin to what we are doing now, have again and again been submitted to this parliament by a separate vote. Therefore I see no wrong in these railways being treated separately.

C.N.R.-Construction
There is the further point, the reason for that. Let us take as an illustration the resolution on the order paper to loan $10,000,000 to the Montreal Harbour Commission. Here is a case in which we are not going to vote the money year by year in the estimates. We are enacting a law; providing the required amount; we do not limit the harbour board to a particular sum for one year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the Finance Minister permit a question which will bring the matter to a point? Will the minister tell us why it was wrong in 1919 to provide authority to the government to advance money for the construction of railways, for the National lines, and why it is right to do it by legislation in 1923?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not quite recall
what happened in 1919.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have Hansard and the bill here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As far as my impression is concerned I do recollect the question. However, I do not want to dwell unduly on this matter. Is it not a reasonable proposition that instead off asking for money each year provision should be made for carrying on the work continuously? These railways are not to be completed in one year, neither is the harbour of Montreal. In both cases we vote a sum estimated to be sufficient for the purpose, and if it is not expended in one year it is expended in another. In both cases parliament has given the necessary authority. All that my right hon. friend has said regarding the authority of parliament is complied *with in this resolution. We have a distinct vote for a distinct purpose, we have a distinct limitation of amount, and what more can be asked? The Minister of Railways pointed out that if you limit the amount to a sum for the particular year you may stop the operations at the end of the twelve months. As long as you have designated the roads [DOT] to be constructed, as long as the terminal points are indicated, as long as the amount is limited, what earthly good is to be accomplished in the month of December by telling the Minister of Railways that he must stop and not do anything more? It is not reason, it is not law, it is not common sense.

I listened very carefully to the reading of the section of the Railway Act by the leader of the Opposition which applies, and I am forced to say that I came to the same conclusion that the Minister of Finance has just stated-there is a very specific provision that the money shall be voted by parliament. I can find nothing in the statute which requires that the money shall be voted year by year. I should just like to remark parenthetically that some very wonderful things must have been taking place in parliament in years gone by judging from the remarks we have heard from the leader of the Opposition. However, I for one am not so much interested in what was right or what was wrong in 1919. What I want to know is whether it is right or wrong to carry out what we are interested in at the present time; and I cannot see anything in the act-

However, I want to remain within the strict reading of the law and if the leader of the Opposition is right in his contention that what is proposed here is against the law, of course, we will bow to the decision.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

Just a word in answer to what the Minister of Finance has said. He claims that our position is not sense, is not law; I do not know how much further he went, I simply remember that much. Now, let me read what the present Prime Minister said on this subject. His words are to be found at page 1539 of Hansard for 1919. He said:
If parliament wishes to part with the last vestige of the control that it has over the executive, we should pass this clause, but if parliament wishes to retain any control it may have over expenditures this clause should not be permitted to stand. If money is needed for the carrying on or improvement of the Grand Trunk system, let the minister come to parliament, just as the government does in regard to vother appropriations that may be necessary, state in parliament what money he needs and have that money voted by parliament
C.N.R.-C (instruction

I do not think it is too strong a term to say that this section is thoroughly vicious in that it deprives parliament altogether of its control over the supplies that may be necessary for this purpose. Under this term "the operation or improvement of the Grand Trunk system" the minister can spend public money for any conceivable purpose in connection with these roads, building hotels, branch lines and stations; he can go into any constituency in this Dominion where the railway is going -to run and find that this particular t-own needs this improvement or that particular county needs that improvement-
And so on. That is what the Prime Minister thought in 1919.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There has been a change of government since then.
There has been a change of government, yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A different government altogether.

The ideas my right hon. friend had when he was here are absolutely and entirely different from the ideas he holds now that he is over there. What was absolutely wrong when he was sitting here is absolutely right when he is sitting on the treasury benches. What was practically misappropriation of public funds when he was in opposition becomes a public duty entitling him to make the expenditure when he sits there as leader of the government. Of course it is a different government. That is the whole point. It is not necessary to argue this matter any further. The Prime Minister himself gives the House the answer: He was here before, he is over there now. The facts are the same. Surely they are the same to this extent at any rate: It is a first rate thing for the country as a whole, and for parliament, to know exactly what we are spending on railways, to know each twelve months where we stand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Is that not
exactly what the Minister of Railways is doing?

Not at all, that is exactly what the minister is getting away from. We might just as well be clear on that point; there is the whole question. Previously we had to have our twelve months' programme which covered everything including deficits and construction. My hon. friend's bill this year covers construction just as it did before but we will not get the complete annual statement as we formerly did. Under the estimates parliament has got some control, but under this bill we shall have none. This policy will enable the government to do in the constituencies exactly what was foretold

by the Prime Minister when he was in opposition. There are twenty-eight constituencies in which they can do practically what they like. Supposing an election comes on? I do not believe there is any prospect of an immediate election, but supposing there was?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: You never can tell.

Here is the very vehicle for the government's purpose, here is the bait which can be dangled here and there. Parliament has the right to know what is to be done each year and has the right to vote money for the purposes of this undertaking. But that right has gone. If parliament wants to do this all right, but let parliament clearly understand what it is doing. The customary practice, the right and proper practice is being changed and the minister will be in a position to say "I am not bound by the approximations given to parliament. The
6 p.m. mileage of these lines are mere approximations, the amounts of money to be spent are mere approximations. I can do as I like, under those approximations, with the credit of this country."

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I just want to inform my hon. friend that what he has read is not consistent with this bill at all, not in the least. If he will look further into the matter, and calmly, he will find that parliament is making the appropriation, that stated amounts are to be expended every year, and that a full report must be made to parliament of the money expended.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: After it is spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Parliament then has the right to say what further shall be done and if we should overrun certain amounts parliament will have to provide for that.
If they are overrun.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No deviation, no thwarting of the power or will of parliament, directly or indirectly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What option has parliament if the money is overrun or spent? How does parliament exercise any control after the money is spent and gone? This is the Scribe Hotel case over again.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
My right hon. friend is raising a very small point. If everybody is dishonest, crooked, then the thing may go wrong; but if people are fairly honest, with the check of parliament, they will not gt>
C.N.R.-Construction
wrong. Let me point this out. My hon. friend said that this is against the law. This bill in getting its third reading, will be the law when it passes through this House.

I can see a very good reason from a logical point of view, why this amendment should not carry. Supposing we pass this amendment, each year an appropriation must be voted to carry on construction for the year. We will vote enough this year to make the surveys on these different lines. It is now fairly late in the season, and it is possible that not more than a survey will be made this year. Next year we must vote money for the construction that it is expected we shall be able to carry out during the year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Vote it this year.

This means that this House will be in session until August. That is a possibility. There is also a possibility that no construction will take place next year. I am in favour of voting the three-years' programme. I am certainly in favour of this parliament voting money to carry on public works, and I can see an object in voting the supply for the three-years' programme, for the reasons I have given.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister for a word of explanation before the vote is called.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What is the explanation that my hon. friend wants?
The Prime Minister has made in the past certain representations which are alleged to be inconsistent with his position today, and I should like some explanation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are not inconsistent. If my hon. friend will carefully read all that has been said to-day, he will find that there is no inconsistency.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Canadian National Railways Act, 1919, and to provide that no securities as defined in section 26 of the said act, including in such definition equipment certificates or obligations in any form intended to be issued to the public, shall be issued, except those approved as to form, terms and amount by the Governor in Council, and that such securities so approved may be guaranteed by His Majesty.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee on the resolution, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of this resolution is to restrict in some respects the powers of the Canadian National Railway Company. The numerous companies now comprising the Canadian National Railway system have their independent charters, under which certain borrowing powers are conferred. .These charters are still outstanding; some of the borrowing powers remain unused, and if we take no action whatever it would be within the power of the Canadian National Railway Company to exercise those borrowing powers. What we propose in the first place by this resolution is that no such security shall be issued under those old borrowing powers without the consent of the Governor in Council. In the second place, where they have the lawful right to issue securities and where that issue is approved by the Governor in Council, in that case the Governor in Council shall have the power to guarantee them. It is not likely that those old borrowing powers will be very largely used, because the later legislation confers borrowing powers-both the Canadian National Railway Act of 1919 and the act with which we have been dealing today. A bond or security of any kind now issued by the Canadian National Railway Company is to all intents and purposes a bond of the government of Canada; it is desirable, therefore, that we should recognize that fact in the placing of securities. As I say, it is not anticipated that these borrowing powers will be used extensively; perhaps they will be used quite rarely if at all, but if they are used it will be only with the consent of the Governor in Council, and if bonds are to be

C.N.R.-Securities
issued for any lawful purposes there is no reason why they should not then be guaranteed by the Governor in Council.
Have any bonds of this character yet been issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have not been issued by the Canadian National Railway Company, but the various subsidiary companies have of course issued bonds in many cases.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I must say I sought in vain to understand this resolution before the minister rose, and now in the light of his explanation my difficulty is enhanced. The minister says that the different companies composing the National system have by virtue of the original charters, which they held prior to the passing of the Canadian National Railway Act, certain borrowing powers, and that he wishes to curtail those borrowing powers by placing upon them a restraint, the restraint being that the forms and so forth must first be approved-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And the propriety.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Well, the resolution does not say so. It simply says, "approved as to form, terms and amount." But that is not the point I am making. The restraint he intends to impose upon these constituent companies who want to issue bonds or place mortgages in pursuance of their old charter powers is that such issue or mortgage shall first have the approval of the Governor in Council, and once that approval is given the Governor in Council is to have the power of guaranteeing those bonds. Well, my first point is that the resolution does not do that at all. I hope the minister can correct me-or rather, I shall be very much interested if he can; I have not much hope. What does the resolution say? It reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Canadian National Railway Act, 1919, and to provide that no securities as defined in section 26 of the said act, including in such definition equipment certificates or obligations in. any form intended to be issued to the public, shall be issued, except those approved as to form, terms and amount by the Governor in Council, and that such securities so approved may be guaranteed by His Majesty.
I direct the minister's attention to the fact that what he is doing is resolving to amend the Canadian National Railway Act, section 26, so as to provide that any securities issued under that section must be submitted to him. Now, what is section 26? It reads:
The company may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, issue bonds, debentures, debenture stock, perpetual or terminable, or other securities. . . in repect of the mileage of the lines of railway which it, from time to time, constructs, acquires, owns or
controls,-'not including the Canadian Government Railways, nor exceeding, with outstanding securities, in the aggregate $75,000 per mile. Such securities may be issued separately in respect of one or more of the company's lines of railway or properties, or in respect of all of its lines, or properties taken together. The company may issue such securities in one or more separate series maturing at the same date or at separate dates, and bearing the same rate or different rates of interest, not exceeding in any case six per cent, and may limit the security for any series or issue to such of the franchises, property, assets, rents and revenues of the company, present or future, or both, as are described in the mortgage or mortgages made to secure such securities.
I have read it hurriedly, but does the minister catch the point? Here is a section which says the Canadian' National Railway Company may issue securities, and it may issue them on the whole Canadian National Railway property or on only part of the property, but they are an issue of the Canadian National Railway Company. It is the Canadian National Railway Company that issues them and undertakes to pay. The security may be on the whole property or on only part, and the minister says it is expedient to amend that so that these securities may be submitted to the Governor in Council. Does he not see that does not affect in the least any security issued irrespective of the Canadian National Railway Act by virtue of the charter powers of one of the companies making up the composite company? It does not affect that at all. He is only touching the securities here, and the Canadian National Railway Company cannot issue a security save as it has authority to do so by the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The old constituent companies will not issue these securities now because all their powers are transferred and consolidated with the Canadian National Railway, and therefore any securities issued would be issued by the Canadian National Railway, but we were advised that there was quite a possibility that the power outstanding would authorize the Canadian National Railway, in virtue of the consolidation of the various constituent companies, to issue securities. At all events it was thought well to make it sure that if any securities were to be issued they should be made subject to the Governor in Council. It may be that we are simply making assurance doubly sure, but the legal officers thought that such action was desirable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have not struck the section yet, but I am satisfied that there is a section here already which says that all securities issued by the company shall be approved as to form and so forth by the Governor in

C.N.R.-Securities
Council. That is in all these things. Very well, the minister has that now. It does not matter whether he has it under the old powers or not. As a matter of fact, I do not care what anyone says; it is too obvious to admit of discussion. The Canadian National Railway Company cannot issue a security unless it is authorized by the act creating the company. It is given certain powers by that act and it cannot get powers from any other company. It is created by a single act, and these powers it exercises in issuing securities are restrained already by the very terms embodied in this resolution. Consequently it seems to me the minister is not doing what he set out to do. It may be he is restraining the parent company, but he is not restraining the constituent companies at all, and my opinion is that he is not restraining anything. I will tell you what the minister is doing in this resolution. He is doing just what he did this afternoon or what his colleague to his right fMr. Graham) did. He is just preparing another bill by which this government can guarantee the bonds of the Canadian National Railway Company and not come to parliament for a vote for the purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is dreaming. There is not a shadow of foundation for that view. It may be that this is unnecessary, that we already have the power, but the idea that there is any object here of issuing any securities not authorized by parliament is entirely mistaken. All the rights, powers and privileges of the constituent companies I think have been transferred and consolidated in the Canadian National Railway Company. It has been thought expedient to retain all these rights, powers and privileges, but it has been held and with some force that inasmuch as all these rights, powers and privileges have been transferred and consolidated with the Canadian National Railway Company it might have power to issue securities under the borrowing powers of these constituent companies. The most that can be said is that this bill may be unnecessary. There may be something in that view, but the idea that there is any object of issuing securities not authorized hy parliament is entirely mistaken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We will just see. The Canadian National Railway Company cannot take powers from these other companies. It has not the power to take them. There is no power save what is here. Secondly, the other companies cannot give the powers to them. A federal railway like the Canadian Northern -all of them are federal railways that are in the act, under the provisions of the British 
North America Act-not one of these can transfer its powers save with the consent of parliament. They cannot do it. The Canadian National Railway Company to-day has not any of the powers of these subsidiairy companies except as given to it by this act. To my mind this is pure surplusage. In fact I must say I think it is merely an attempt to cover up the real purpose of this resolution. The minister says, not without the consent of parliament. That is all right. But what he is going to do is to bring down a bill to enable guarantees to be given on the Canadian Northern securities, and once he gets that bill through he can go right ahead guaranteeing them and giving the credit of this country, and he does not need to include the amount in the estimates. Now we will watch his bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We do not need to include the amount in the estimates, but we would in the proper appropriation. If my hon. friend finds in this some mysterious deep-laid scheme I can only come to the conclusion that he has allowed his intense partisanship to lead him astray. There is not a shadow of foundation for anything of the sort. It may be surplusage. It does not create any power, but if there is an existing power to issue securities of the Canadian National Railway then this says that if they are lawful securities the Governor in Council may guarantee them. It may be that my hon. friend is right and that this is covered by the act of 1919. He may be correct in that view, and if he simply argues that this legislation is unnecessary and that we have covered it already that is worthy of consideration. But when he imagines there is some deep-laid diabolical scheme to guarantee something and give the government new powers I can only hope that he will not always see these mysteries in the common things of life. If he takes the view that it is covered by existing legislation, that view is entitled to respect, but I hope he is not going to base any argument on the foolish assumption that there is some dark, deep-laid scheme behind this legislation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will bring in the bill.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Fielding thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 244, to amend the Canadian National Railways Act, 1919.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
1.	That *the Minister of Finance may make advances to the chartered banks and to the savings banks to which the Quebec Savings Bank Act, 1913, applies by the issue of Dominion notes upon the pledge of certain securities, such advances to be repayable within one year with interest at such rate as may be from time to time fixed by the treasury board.
2.	That the provisions of the proclamation dated 3rd September, 1914, made under the authority of the Finance Act, 1914, so far as they authorize the chartered banks to make payments in their notes instead of in. gold or Dominion notes, and so far as they suspend the redemption in gold of Dominion notes be continued in force for a period not exceeding three years after the date of the coming into force of any enactment founded on this resolution; provided that the Governor in Council by proclamation may declare and proclaim an earlier date for the termination of any enactment which may be founded on this resolution ; and
3.	That the Governor in Council during a period not exceeding three years after the date of the coming into force of any enactment founded on this resolution may by proclamation from time to time and for any period or periods declare and proclaim that the export of gold coin, gold bullion and fine gold bars from the Dominion of Canada shall be prohibited except in such cases as may be deemed desirable by the Minister of Finance and under licenses to be issued by him; provided that the Governor in Council by proclamation may declare and proclaim an earlier date for the termination of any enactment which may be founded on this resolution.
Motion agreed to and House went into committee, Mr. Gordon, in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The object of this resolution, Mr. Chairman, is to renew what is called the Finance Act of 1914. That is the act under which the government are authorized to make advances to banks as against certain securities. The act was adopted as a war measure, and no doubt was exceedingly useful in the financial operations during the war. It may be said that the war being over we no longer have any need for the act, but experience has shown that the act is still
required; indeed, I am inclined to think that something of the kind will have to become almost a permanent part of our financial system. Under the act as it stands to-day, the act as passed some years ago, the government are authorized to advance to the various chartered banks, and to the banks mentioned in the act, sums of money as against certain securities not specified but left to the judgment of the treasury board. Any securities of which the treasury board may approve can be accepted for the purpose, and the government can make advances against them. This resolution, and the bill to be founded thereon, simply renews the act but is a little more specific: Instead of leaving the whole matter to the treasury board the resolution and the bill will indicate the classes of securities upon which advances should be made. The securities of the higher class beyond all question are acceptable. Then we come to the class of securities as to which there may be more room for question. We do not need any particular advice or consultation respecting the standing of the higher class of securities-the high class Imperial government securities, the Dominion, provincial and municipal securities; but there is also a class included in the general expression of what I may call commercial securities. Therein comes a little trouble. My impression is that when the act was passed it was hardly contemplated that these commercial securities should be used; I think the act was designed to serve another purpose, But there is no machinery in the Finance department for making inquiries into the character of securities of that class. As I said a moment ago we do not need any machinery to know the value of certain high class securities such as Dominion and provincial securities, or high class municipal securities, we can all easily ascertain the value of these; but when we come to what are called commercial securities, commercial paper and securities like that, machinery for determining their value does not exist. I am inclined to think, although that is a mere matter of opinion, that originally it was not intended that these securities should be used in a large way. However, they are to-day a part of our financial system and there is a growing feeling, perhaps, that there should be some method of rediscounting such as this act provides for. Having in view that class of securities we aim at seeking the advice of somebody who is competent to advise. As I stated before, we have no organized machinery in the Finance department for that purpose, and we
Finance Act, 1904

are proposing in this bill that the gentlemen who are trustees of what is called the Central Gold Reserve institution-which was pretty much discussed in the Banking and Commerce committee-shall be deemed an advisory committee and that we shall have the right to ask their advice. They are not to control the matter, but we may at any time ask their advice as to the character of securities that are offered. Again I say we do not need their advice in the case of the higher class of securities; but if some of the banks were to ask us to make advances against ordinary commercial securities it might be desirable that we should have some means of making inquiry into the character of those securities. As the best available means we propose to ask the gentlemen who represent the government and the banks as trustees for the Central Gold Reserve. We regard them practically as an advisoi-y committee from whom we may seek advice if it be needed.
Another portion of the bill relates to the proclamations by which the export of gold is forbidden. We propose, for the present, to continue the powers to prohibit the export of gold, with the addition that if at any moment it may be deemed necessary, that power can be waived and the export of gold continued. These are the main features of the resolution and of the bill which is to be founded upon it.

I think my
hon. friend is absolutely right in continuing the operation of the War Finance Act. It is something that has proved its value time and time again, and I know that the minister needs it to-day in order to keep commerce going upon a proper basis. In connection with the origin of the act it is, I think, quite true that the securities mainly looked upon as securities likely to be offered were not only our own and provincial securities but other first class securities which became available during the war period, namely, the certificates and notes of the Imperial government against which many loans were made. But besides that there was a very direct object, and that object was the discounting of paper covering the wheat movement. That, of course, is really just as good a security as any of these other securities. We only lend to a proportion of the whole amount covered in these wheat and flour transactions, and we are protected by the usual bills of lading, warehouse receipts, insurance and the like. I hope my hon. friend is not, through any advisory committee, seeking to curtail the TMr. Fielding.]
activities under the act having regard to the movement of the wheat crop. I think I am perfectly within the mark in telling the committee that we never had a loss in connection with the operations under the act. I think my hon. friend will agree with me that we have had some pretty bad times to go through in connection with the war, and the deflation period after the war. But we have had no losses and, speaking frankly, I do not think any very great difficulties. II desire to see the minister doing nothing which removes direct government supervision and control of the extension of these credits. I do not know why the act is necess'ary at all to deal with the question of an advisory committee. If my hon. friend, in the discharge of the office, thinks he has to get advice it is always open to him to get it, but I think the responsibility always lies with the department-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely.

-as to either
the granting or the refusal of credit. I repeat, this is a resolution which I think ought to be adopted, and I hope that the main object will be kept clearly in view-that this is a government function with government responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I entirely concur in what my hon. friend has said. The government cannot and do not desire to absolve themselves of responsibility and if my hon. friend will look at the bill-
I have not seen the bill yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-he will find that special reference is made there to the class of securities that are regarded as favourable:
Promissory notes and bills of exchange secured by documentary title to wheat, oats, rye, barley, corn, buckwheat, flax or other commodity;
Then the bill goes on to say:
Promissory notes and bills of exchange issued or drawn for agricultural, industrial, or commercial purposes and which have been used or are to be used for such purposes.
It is not intended for a single moment that the government shall absolve themselves of any responsibility, but they may need information as to that class of securities.
As I stated before, we have in the department no organized machinery to deal with them. All the power we take is this. I will give an illustration. Supposing a bank offered us some security which might be of a very

Finance Act, 1904
good character, but of which we had not the knowledge. Of course anybody in a business way can ascertain the value of securities of the higher class; but if securities of a less substantial character were offered, it might be desirable that we should get some information as to their character. We have thought that these four bankers in Montreal could be for that purpose an advisory committee. That does not mean that they are to have any responsibility or that we evade responsibility. It means that if we need information as to the particular class of security, we do not know of any better authority from whom we can ask information than the gentlemen indicated. They do not have the responsibility. We have the responsibility and must take it. This is merely a precaution in 'the case of a possible offering of a certain class of securities, which may be all right but concerning which we require information. Otherwise, I agree entirely with the hon. member for West York that the object is just as he has described it, and our purpose is not to restrict the business which is being done under this measure.

Is it not a fact that what the minister proposes to do is already being done in the United States by the creation of the Federal Reserve Bank system, and that all these things are being done there? There is absolute need of a similar institution in this country. For the first time the minister has admitted the need of something of that kind in Canada. I have in my hand a memorandum-
Read it.

I have no intention of reading it, but I will send the Minister of Finance a copy. It gives the details of the splendid machinery that has been created in the United States for this very purpose. This is not exactly in the hands of the banks; but it is in the hands of the government; they take charge of it, and the Secretary of the Treasury and the Treasury department are all parties to it. They discount great quantities of prime paper for the banks for all kinds of organizations; the banks get this money at a very low rate of interest, and they are in a position to increase the amount available that they can offer to the public also at a low rate of interest. If we adopt something like that, we have a first class system to deal with the question, and to reduce the rate of interest to the country on the prime securities of the country. This
is being done in England, and almost every country is gradually coming to this system. All the evidence now is, that the National Reserve Bank system of the United States is an absolute necessity for that country; that it secures discounts for everybody entitled to them at a low rate of interest, and that national notes take largely the place of bank notes, in order to give this credit to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no doubt this
measure serves to some extent the same purpose as the national reserve system of the United States. But as we are not likely at this session to adopt the national reserve system generally, we might have this bill as a piece of it, possibly.

The national
reserve system was a thing that was very carefully considered, and it has not cost a great deal of money. Running it in the way we ran it before-and I think my hon. friend will probably continue to run it in the same way-the cost to the country is practically nothing; there has been just a little more clerical work to be done. On the question of interest, it may be interesting to the committee to know that during the whole of the war period at the time these things were being done, the rate of interest which was charged to Canadian customers, varied from 1 to li and sometimes as much as 2 per cent less than the same charge being exacted by American banks. The whole thing was done cheaply.

What is the basis on which the amount of these advances is decided? Would a weak financial condition of a bank, it being therefore much in need, be a factor? If so, how would it operate? Would it tend to increase the advance or to lessen it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a margin of safety, but at the moment I have forgotten what it is. We make a safe reserve in that :espect. We do not advance the full face value, but I cannot tell my hon. friend offhand what proportion we keep. I think that answers the first question. The advantage of that was that we would certainly get the money and get it at the beginning. It was contemplated that' the tax should be paid, for example, by the importer at the beginning and after he had passed the goods on to the manufacturer he would be entitled to refund, because we would then follow the goods into the manufactory and get the tax at the final stage. That would work out, in a way, successfully from the point of view of the government, but it was urged that it would impose a considerable burden on business men; that where large transactions were being carried on, the necessity for financing to meet the additional duties required would be a serious matter. But perhaps even more serious was the representation that in making arrangements for the refund there would be considerable trouble. After full consideration and hearing the many conflicting views on the subject we came to the conclusion that we would not insist upon the payment of the tax at the time of the importation of the goods; that if the importer sold the goods to a licensed manufacturer there need be no tax paid at that stage; we would follow the goods into the hands of the licensed manufacturer and on his completing the transaction and producing something to be sold the tax would be levied then. I think the change that is made is fairly acceptable-I will not say universally acceptable, because no system of taxation can come under that category. But I am quite sure that although there are differences of opinion on the subject, this form is the most acceptable to the business people.
Have the business men expressed their view in the matter?
