speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I did complain and do
still about the way this has been done. I doubt if there are three hon. members of this House who know what they are doing right now. I do not, and what is more I doubt whether the minister himself does. The tortuous career of this sales tax and its hopeless involutions would baffle the intellect of anybody. The minister took a sales tax that was simple, that was working all right, and he not only piled conditions on it but he kept changing and shifting and backing and filling, and finally placed the whole incidence of the tax on the importer. Other features were changed, but as to that feature the next change was the provision in some way that the importer should pay the tax first and that there should then be some rebate system when the goods reached the ultimate manufacturer. It is the latter that is being repealed, as I grasp it, by this legislation; that is to say, the final circle the minister traversed is being retraversed backwards. What are we to do? The minister says it is all right; that it is acceptable, but what does it mean? This is the proviso we are adding now; I will read it:
Provided that the consumption or sales tax specified in this section shall not be payable on goods exported; or on goods sold by a licensed manufacturer or producer to another licensed manufacturer or producer if the goods are to be used in, wrought into, or attached to articles to be manufactured or produced for sale and which are articles subject to the consumption or sales tax, or on goods imported by a licensed manufacturer or producer if the goods are to be used in, wrought into, or attached to articles to be manufactured or produced for sale and which are articles subject to the consumption or sales tax; or on goods imported by a licensed wholesaler or jobber whose sales are to be accounted for under the provisions of subsection (7); or on goods sold by a licensed manufacturer or producer to a licensed wholesaler or jobber whose sales are to be accounted for under the provisions of subsection seven of this section.
Well, what is left? Something may be left, but I do not know what it is. Why not simply say that in respect of importations to be used in manufacture there shall not be a tax levied until the manufacture reaches its final state? But if it is impossible to do it that way-I know how simple it is until you get into the details-why not tabulate these exceptions so that they will be clear to the mind? If they were tabulated alphabetically, assuming it is essential that we go into all these matters in order to get back to where we were, the thing might be a little more easily understood. In fact, it is hopelessly involved legislation, and I fancy the working out of it is going to be involved. Indeed, I question whether the minister is going to put this legislation into effect. It is to be

deferred until the first of January of next year. Well, his conduct last year was similar with respect to that beet tax; he finally did not put it into effect at all. And when he puts into effect a six per cent sales tax levied at the source and faces the ultimate result of his conduct, I should not wonder if he would quail before it. But if he intends to put it into effect surely it is possible not only to arrive at what we are finally legislating by a direct and immediate route but to express it in clear language. We have arrived at this stage by all sorts of marches forward, marches back, marches in and marches out and up and down; why, it is almost worthy of the Minister of Agriculture and his oleomargarine record. And if the business man finally knows what his position in the matter is-well, 1 do not think many hon. members of this House do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is one point on which my right hon. friend is certainly wrong. He said we took the simple tax that existed and changed it into this incomprehensible thing. I can assure him that the form of the tax was not simple; it was the subject of a great deal of discussion and a great deal of objection. The tax was payable at several stages, something at one stage and something at another. It was a new question, no doubt the ministers in charge of it made an earnest effort to make it simple, but as a matter of fact it was not simple. As to the proposed change, while it may cause a little friction at the beginning, as all new taxes do, I believe in the end it should work out well. There are good reasons for delay in putting the tax into effect, reasons based on the convenience of business men. I assure my right hon. friend that his judgment is hurried in regard to the drafting. The drafting of measures of this kind is always done under the advice of officials of experience, not only in general drafting but in the administration of customs laws, and I would yield to their judgment rather than to my own so far as the drafting is concerned. This drafting which my right hon. friend thinks is unwise has been well considerod; we are advised by those most competent that it will serve its purpose. The delay is justified by good business reasons, and I have no doubt that if we are both spared to come here in a subsequent session my right hon. friend will find the tax in operation and I hope it will be working smoothly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister was told the same thing when he made the last change

War Revenue Act
imposing the tax on the importer. He was advised that it would work smoothly, but it was so obviously impractical and unsound that I do not know what kind of advisers the minister has. Why, it immediately raised a storm all over the Dominion, and the minister at once surrendered. I do not know which change this is as to number. After this I think we ought to pay no attention to the first three or four or five budgets but wait until we get the sixth and then deal with it.

I have received protests from business men against the tax as it now exists. The net result probably of this is that we are adopting a rather vicious principle, and if we are going to have a deferred sale tax the first thing we know there will be an agitation in the country for deferred customs duties. That would lead us to a condition of affairs that would be very annoying, and instead of securing revenue for the government it would postpone the payment until it gets right down to the consumer.

I would really like to understand something about this. As to the first tax I do not know that there was very much difficulty about that as soon as it got going, and I never heard of any difficulty as to just what the law meant. There was a tax on the manufacturer and a tax on the wholesaler. There was a tax on the retailer and so far as the first law itself was concerned when we had it down in the low brackets there was very little of it passed on to the public, in fact, nothing was passed on at all. But what my hon. friend has done in this case, and if I am wrong he will tell me, is simply to adopt Mr. Tinling's paper. Mr. Tinling really is the author of this tax. Mr. Tinling worked out the percentages. He has a tax of six per cent that he works out himself, then he has another tax of 6i or 7 per cent. The whole thing has been worked out entirely for my hon. friend by Mr. Tinling. As I understood the first suggestion it was briefly something like this, that we have a consumption or sales tax of six per cent on the sales price of all goods produced or manufactured, and that the tax be paid by the producer or manufacturer at the time of the sale by him. That was the broad principle we started with. I was not here the other day when the sales tax discussion was on, but there is a question which is immediately provoked right at the commencement of our consideration which perhaps my hon. friend has covered already. We have been to some extent getting away from the intermediary
distributor. Quite a number of producers now sell directly to retailers. There is always a difference in price between what is sold to the retailer and what is sold to the jobber.
I think it would be fair to say that what would be sold to the jobber at 80, taking that for the sake of illustration, would be sold to the retailer at 100 approximately. What is my hon. friend going to do having regard to this tax being imposed as it is at the source? Is the tax to be paid on the 80, which would be the value of the article as sold to the jobber, and which would make a tax of $4.80, or will there be another tax on the same article when sold to the retailer, based of course upon the higher price? If that is done it is going to throw out the trade lists between the jobbers and the retailers, where you would have a tax on the same article in the first instance of $4.80 and of $6 in the second instance. Before going on I would like my hon. friend to tell me if that point has been considered, and what will be the stand taken by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that there are many questions that he can ask as to interpretation which I should hesitate to answer because I quite understand that it is a matter where a difference of opinion may easily arise. Section 19bbb I am advised meets the point my hon. friend raises. It reads:
In addition to any duty or tax that may be payable under this part, or any other statute or law, there shall be imposed, levied and collected a consumption or sales tax of six per cent on the sale place of all goods produced or manufactured in Canada, including the amount of excise duties when the goods are sold in bond, which tax shall be payable by the producer or manufacturer at the time of the sale thereof by him; and in the case of imported goods the like tax upon the duty paid value of the goods imported payable by the importer or transferee who takes the goods out of bond for consumption at the time when the goods are imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption.
For the purpose of calculating the amount of the consumption or sales tax, "sale price" shall mean the price before any amount payable in respect of the consumption or sales tax is added thereto.
I think that covers the point raised by my hon. friend.

Oh no, my hon. friend's adviser has not got the point at all, and it is something which would occur to aDy business man right at the very commencement of his . consideration of this tax. I am right in saying that you have sales of the same article to jobbers on the one hand and to retailers on the other. I know I am also right in saying that you have your regular trade lists, and to keep faith with the jobber
War Revenue Act

on the one hand and the retailer on the other certain margins are maintained. Now let me go over it again because the minister evidently did not catch my point at all. We will assume that the sale price to the jobber is 80, and the sale price to the retailer 100. On the face of it, it would appear that the tax on the article when sold to the jobber is to be $4.80, and when sold to the retailer $6. Now that is going to throw out the alignment at once. What my hon. friend so far has not told me and what I want to know is if that same article is going to bear different sales taxes or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they have different prices I should think the tax could be levied on the actual selling price. The minister has in this case as in the case of the customs law a very general power to deal with any question of valuation, but it is a very intricate matter and I would rather not attempt to interpret the act. If there be any room for doubt in the matter I would have it inquired into, but I would not give my hon. friend a definite answer to his questions because it is quite possible there is room for a difference of opinion as to the interpretation.

I would have thought it would have occurred to anyone before we put new legislation on the books that we should have some .idea of how it is going to work out, and the point I have raised is the very first, thing that occurs to the business man. What is going to happen in connection with his lists? It is not a question of varying prices. The prices are stable, they are the same. You have your jobbers' lists and you have your retailers' lists. Now if my hon. friend is going to say that he is going to charge a different sales tax rate when sold to the retailer as compared with the rate when sold to the jobber it simply means that he is putting still further difficulties in the way of cutting out any intermediaries and cutting down the cost of distribution. If it be that in addition to getting lower trade prices, which the jobber always gets, he is going to pay on the same article a lower sales tax than the retailer, then of course the government is certainly not helping the retailer who desires to buy directly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It appears to me that the selling price in each case would determine the tax, but if any peculiar circumstances arise which make the matter one of difficulty there is a clause here giving the minister

power to determine the value for taxation purposes. It reads:
Whenever goods are manufactured or produced in Canada under such circumstances or conditions as render it difficult to determine the value thereof for the consumption or sales tax because,-
(a)	a lease of such goods or the right of using the same but not the right of property therein is sold or given; or,
(b)	such goods having a royalty imposed thereon, the royalty is uncertain, or is not from other causes a reliable means of estimating the value of the goods; or,
(c)	such goods ace manufactured by contract for labour only and not including the value of the goods that enter into the same, or under any other unusual or peculiar manner or conditions; or,
(d)	such goods are for use by the manufacturer or producer and not for sale
the minister may determine the value for the tax under this act.
In other words whenever any of these difficulties arise that my hon. friend has in mind, the minister has the power of fixing the valuation on which the tax shall be levied.

The minister
having read those paragraphs will surely agree that the case I mentioned has not been touched at all. There is not a single provision in the cases read by the minister himself where any case such as I have just given him could be considered. I have not given him complex cases but the easiest ones that could possibly arise in the administration of the act, a matter of every day business, whether we are to have two sales taxes on the same standard article or not. We have not had a single thing even suggested one way or the other as to what is to happen. It is on a par, I suppose, with the general miasma which seems to surround this new proposal. We cannot get the facts in connection with the first case so let us take the next one: Manufacturers or producers of over $10,000 annually are to be licensed. I take it from that, and I want the minister to interrupt me if I am wrong, that the fact of this licensing would enable these manufacturers or producers originally, if licensed, to import without the payment of any fee in advance? They are bonded and the like.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, the power of the minister is certainly very considerable, but he can only apply the act as it reads. I do not think it admits of the minister exercising any power in a manner unjust to any of them.

It seems to me that we have in the first place, a declaration, that people have to be licensed to do a certain amount of business. Then we have a declaration in the next instance that the manufacturers of goods, which when sold are liable to sales tax, will have to take out this license when the minister says so. As it is now left, it is a matter entirely for the Customs department to say whether a man doing a business under $10,000 is to pay or not. The minister may select any one he chooses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the conditions set forth here.
What conditions? Mr. FIELDING: I have just read them.

It is simply to this extent: using goods exempt from the sales tax. That might be construed in one instance to apply to use of goods to the extent of one per cent and in another instance to the use of goods to the extent of 50 per cent. The minister might say "I do not care to apply it to this particular trade, I am going to apply it to that trade." The whole thing is wide open. It is more than order in council taxation, it is taxation by the minister himself, just as he wants to tax in connection with all these smaller matters.

Are we on section 6 of this bill?
War Revenue Act
We started out on section 1 but we have jumped to section 6.

I have received a large number of telegrams and communications from manufacturers in the Niagara district referring to this sales tax. I am anxious to have the bill discussed section by section, and explanations given by the minister, so that we may explain the matter to the people whom we represent.
We have to get an understanding of the idea first.

I do not see anything myself in that section but we shall never get anywhere if all sections are discussed together in a hotch potch sort of way. I do not want to make any suggestion to my hon. friend as to the course to be pursued. I found the general discussion proceeding on the sales tax and I continued it. We certainly will have a general discussion of this tax on some section of the bill. It was suggested by the Minister of Finance we might just as well go on with it now. It is a matter of indifference to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have drifted into a discussion of the sales tax, and having entered upon it I see no reason why we should not dispose of it.

That seems to me to be proper, too. There is another thing' that we should like to get a little more light on in order to enable us to understand the clause. There is a provision that:
A wholesaler or jobber who sells not less than SO per cent of his total sales of goods to a licensed manufacturer or producer. . . . may be granted an annual license.
It is a matter of importance to the wholesaler or jobber to be able to get his license. The minister will see that he has to carry the interest on the payment he has to make. In the first instance, he has a right to his accounts and the like. How are we going to ascertain whether a man is really doing a business of not less than 50 per cent of his total sales to licensed manufacturers or producers? If we do that, and he sells 50 per cent of his sales this month to his licensees 
and he sells none next month to his licensees, is his license to stop? Is anything going to be done to see that there is continuity in this? What is the idea of the clause? Why should we have it at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In all these matters, regulations will be made by the minister. I quite admit that the bill is a very complicated one, and it requires very careful study. There is something in the statement made by hon. gentlemen opposite that even after we have carefully studied the matter, it is full of trouble. All I can say is that the regulations of the department will cover most of these things, and they will be made intelligently and reasonably with a view of meeting the public desire.
What is the idea of the change from the old basis to this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The old basis was a varied rate of sales tax, and this is a straight 6 per cent tax. That is the main point of difference. The other point of difference was as regards the proposals, and I think it is concerning that that hon. gentlemen have received telegrams recently. The proposal was to put a tax on imports. It was held that while that might possibly be a convenience to the government in getting the money from that source, it was imposing burdens on the business man who would have to finance in order to provide the tax. It was represented, and I think truly, that in many large organizations, materials have to be ordered far in advance of their use. They have to be held, and it was contended that if these business men, having large stocks on hand awaiting the moment to be used, had to finance for paying interest and to carry all the stock at the same time, that in itself was going to be a serious burden. I thought there was force in the contention. There was further a provision that when an importer 'paid the tax and the goods afterwards went into a manufacturing concern, there would be a refund, and it was held that keeping of accounts for this would be a troublesome thing. For these reasons we have abandoned putting the tax on the importer at first, and we have provided that the importer shall not pay the tax if he sells to a licensed manufacturer. The goods will be brought into the licensed factory, and ultimately we shall get the tax when the licensed manufacturer produces something to sell. That is the main point of difference that perhaps the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) had in mind.

There is one feature of
this sales tax to which J should like to direct

War Revenue Act
the attention of the minister, something a little more concrete than what we have been getting for the last hour. The committee will remember that a resolution was passed unanimously that some consideration should be given to publishers of magazines and periodical literature. I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that ,instead of giving any relief to that particular industry, he has increased the sales tax from 2| to 6 per cent. That is just about the last straw that breaks the camel's back. Would it not be possible for the minister to do what he promised us when he brought down the budget originally, that is to say, to remove the sales tax from the newsprint and paper that go into magazines and such publications? That particular industry is in a very desperate state, and it is undoubtedly the case that a magazine could be taken from Toronto or Montreal and published at Buffalo at a lower cost than it could be published at in Canada. I am informed on very good authority that the managers of the largest magazine that we have in Canada are contemplating that particular move. It would not be a very admirable spectacle for the people of Canada to see magazine publishers forced into the United States because of the difficulties and embarrassments that are placed upon them by the laws of this country. Is it too late for the Minister of Finance to revert to his original proposal and to remove the sales tax from the paper and, indeed, from all the materials of magazines? That is a fair proposition. They are paying taxes now; they are paying duty on their art work, on their inks, on everything that goes into the manufacture of magazines and periodical literature. The minister would be well advised if he took that step, and it would be popular throughout the country if he would give that much consideration to the publishing interests. The enormous increase in the cost of production of daily newspapers has caused a great deal of embarrassment, so much that hundreds of daily newspapers have been compelled to suspend publication. Add that feature of the matter to magazines and periodical literature, and I think the case calls for some consideration by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter to which the hon. gentlemen refers, arose - at an earlier stage of the session on a motion which he himself made and which produced an interesting debate. I think it had reference at the time entirely to the customs duty on American periodicals. While there was much to be said in favour of the hon. gentleman's suggestion, there is another side of the question, and we have reason to believe that public opinion on the whole would not favour it. I admit the position of publishers of magazines and periodicals is rather a hard one, but the question of the sales tax is quite a different matter. Magazines and newspapers are now exempt from the sales tax.

Are they exempted on
their raw materials?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the thing they produce. They do not produce raw materials; they produce newspapers and magazines, and they are exempted from the sales tax, while other industries have not that benefit. The raw materials, the newsprint and paper will be produced by the owners of the mills, the paper companies, and they will pay the tax. It is laid down as a principle that with very rare exceptions, all taxes will get down to the ultimate consumer, although you may evade this for a while. In this case, however, the tax is paid by the manufacturer of paper, and not by the publisher, who becomes a seller of magazines, or a seller of newspapers, and who is exempted from the sales tax on those. Of course, it may be said that the paper company passes the sales tax on to the publisher, and I have no doubt that is the case. It would be very pleasant for the Minister of Finance if he could exempt many more things; but I do not think any strong case has been made for the exemption of print and paper; at all events, that was the view which I was obliged to take.

I should like to point out to the minister that the ultimate consumer does not pay this tax, and that it has to be absorbed, not by the papermaker, nor by the ultimate consumer, but by the publisher. When the publisher buys the paper and the sales tax is paid, that sales tax is added to the price of his paper. There can be no doubt about that. It is impossible for the publisher to increase the price of his magazine, and at the same time to get any sale for it. Consequently he has to absorb that extra three and three-quarters per cent in addition to contending against conditions that are already so onerous that it is almost impossible for him to stay in business. This is not like any other industry. If a man is making 'boots, or anything dse, he can pass the tax on to the ultimate consumer; but a man producing a publication of the kind I am describing cannot pass it on. This sales tax is putting an extra burden of three and three-quarters per cent upon the publishing industry instead of giving the relief pleaded for, not only by myself, but by a large number of hon.
War Revenue Act

members, including the Acting Chairman himself (Mr. Marcil). I thought, from the case made out by that hon. gentleman, that we should get that relief, but instead of that there is an added burden. That is the ground of my objection. We have been compelled to accept what the minister says: There cannot be any duty on magazines or on the advertising in magazines. But having accepted that, it is pretty hard now to have the sales tax increased 3J per cent on the raw materials that go into the product, which increase must be absorbed, representing in many cases the difference between solvency and insolvency, or perhaps between the publication of the Canadian magazine in Canada, and in the United States. I still think that the minister should look at this matter sympathetically. I believe he realises that there should be some relief in this direction; in fact I think he has said so. Surely then it is not too late to exempt these publications from the tax on their raw materials. At least do not increase the tax; keep it where it was. Do not add any burden to the industry if you cannot give it the relief for which it asks.
The minister does not say anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What do you expect me to say?

I thought that at least the minister would give us an expression of sympathy if nothing else. I wonder whether he does not yet realize the fact that it is impossible for him to expect this country to carry on in competition with the outside competitor when we have here special heavy burdens thrown upon the producer by a system of taxation to which the outsider is not subject. There was absolutely no answer made by anyone to the figures quoted by the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) when the matter was brought up. There was no dispute about the question; we had the exact facts and figures showing that the business was labouring under a disability. Surely my hon. friend sees perfectly well that when he says that the Canadian magazine must pay a 6 per cent tax on its raw materials, which the American competitor does not pay, he is adding very materially to the burdens of the Canadian publishing business. As I have said before, when discussing this sales tax, I do not believe in a large number of exemptions. My hon. friend must get the money and he has to get it from as broad a field as he can find.
I have never urged exemptions upon him, for I think that possibly our list of exemptions 
to-day is too broad and perhaps the minister has erred in enlarging it. But a very real wrong is done when we get away from the underlying principle of the sales tax. I was responsible for the institution of that tax here and certainly, as I understand it, the underlying principle was that it should be of such a character that its incidence would be so small as, on the one hand, to place no great hardship on business, and on the other render it probable that the tax would not be passed along to the general consuming public. My hon. friend must unquestionably realise that when he gets the tax up to 6 per cent he is losing sight of all that and imposing a burden which is affecting every one of our producers. Let us take my hon. friend's authority in this matter, Mr. Tinling. Mr. Tinling shows that the result of this tax is that the original charge of $6 on a hundred becomes a charge of $11.25. This matter is of sufficient importance to justify some discussion and I will point out to my hon. friend again that in the first instance, under the sales tax of the former government before it received the 50 per cent boost which the hon. gentleman gave it, much of the tax was never passed on. It did not directly add to the cost of living. I gave one or two quotations from the representations of the people that have been importuning my hon. friend to have this change made, namely, the people in business who were anxious to pass on to the consumer 100 per cent of the tax, plus their profits, and I will give one or two other questions. The thing really is so clear that there is no room for argument about it at all. I will take the case of the Wholesale Grocers' Association, whose secretary, Mr. Pyke, was interviewed in connection with the budget.

Where is the hon. member
about to quote from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Somebody had to pay it.
Of course, somebody had to, but the manufacturers were absorbing it.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend
laughs. I will give authorities for my statement.
What did the manufacturers do with it, absorb it into their system or pas's it on?

My hon. friend
may have some confidential advice in regard to the matter, I do not know. This is what the authority-and it is an authority that has been accepted by this government, because
the plan is exactly the plan of Mr. Tinling

says:
That because of the wording and the operating of the act, some manufacturers and the majority of the wholesale and retail trade have been forced to absorb the greater part and in many instances the whole of the sales tax, which has entailed losses aggregating, it is estimated, to about $80,000,000 for these three branches of the trade.
Then he gives details of how it is brought about, and he shows how beautifully it works out when the whole of this tax can be passed on. He shows that the jobbers' profit is 25 per cent-I think he is wrong in his figures, I do not believe it is quite as bad ns shown here because the retail profits are not as high-but he shows the jobber's profit is 25 per cent, the retailer's 50 per cent. Starting with the six dollar tax on a hundred dollars, the jobber's profit at 25 per cent is $1.50, making $7.50; the retailer's profit of 50 per cent on that is $3.75, making a resultant cost to the public, as shown by the author of this plan, of $11.25 to collect a six dollar tax. Obviously, my hon. friend has not had an opportunity of getting at the bottom of this thing, for "he could not answer an elementary question dealing with it only half an hour ago. He will find difficulties without end in connection with it. Just take this one feature. My hon. friend realizing that this is a tremendous tax on industry provides for refunds of all previous taxes. My hon. friend will find when he goes into a warehouse for the purpose of getting at what these refunds are that the tax has gone into the stock, it is not kept in a little box for each special purchase at such-and-such a price. I do not know how my hon. friend is going to find out what those refunds are to commence with. I am sure ample opportunity is being offered there for the bleeding of my hon. friend's department in refunds. There will be practically no check at all. There might be some check if we had constant prices, but we have varying prices right through the year. I think my hon. friend is going to find it something interminable to get at, something very expensive to the country and something impossible to enforce equitably. I hope he will take power to himself to hold up the whole proposition.
Did I understand the minister to say that the tax upon the duty-oaid value of goods is amended so that the duty is not paid when the goods are immediately taken out of bond?

My hon. friend will find

I desire to call the attention of the minister to some matters in regard to which I have received communications. One of them I think he has had under consideration, and perhaps there is to be some change in respect to it. I refer to lumber. Messrs. Haley Bros. Limited, of St. John, write me as follows:
Dear Sir,
Our attention has been drawn to the following provisions in the new sales tax plans as amended May 23,
1923,	as follows:
"(7) A refund of the amount of the said consumption or sales tax may be granted in the following cases,-
(b) To a licensed manufacturer in respect of goods on hand on the 1st of January, 1924, and which are to be used in the production of articles for sale, no refund to be allowed in respect of goods on hand after the 31st of March, 1924."
This provision regarding refund is going to be a hardship to a great many concerns such as ourselves, who have to carry a considerable quantity of material through the winter months, a great deal of which will not be sold until the following fall.
All the lumber which we would normally have on hand January 1st, and on which we have paid a 3 per cent sales tax, it 'would be possible to sell but a small proportion before March 31st, and we would therefore ask you to have this provision removed if possible, or at least the date of same moved forward for six months instead of three as stated in the clause.
Looking at the marginal note it says:
No deduction after 31st May 1924.
But the text reads the 30th day of June,
1924.	I understood that the minister had in mind making some concession in this respect, and I should like to know what may be done. I would further call his attention to the increase from 4J to 6 per cent on lumber. If it were in reference to lumber exported,
I do not know that we would have very much to say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no tax on exports.	[DOT]

I would not have very
much to say if it were a tax on exports, but when we consider that this is a tax upon lumber which enters very largely into the construction of our houses, it becomes very much more serious. This parliament granted for several years considerable assistance, through the vehicle of the provincial governments, for the building of houses. I do not know whether the scheme produced all the results that were expected or not, but undoubtedly there was a good deal of expenditure in most, if not all, of the province. But to-day a man is face to face with the question of erecting his own dwelling, Lumber enters very largely into that and the tax must fall upon the man who intends to

create a home for himself. It is worth while, perhaps, to consider the possibility of letting this tax stand at the old figure. I know the minister is faced with the question of raising revenue; on the other hand the housing problem is very acute especially in our cities. In order that I shall not take up further time later I will direct the attention of the minister to a telegram which I received-I assume he has received similar representations from an important brush manufacturing industry near the city of St. John. These are people who are not unwilling to pay taxes, who want to pay their just share, and I am sure that any objections that they make are put forward not with any idea of embarrassing the administration, but entirely to point out the practical difficulties that would be raised in their business. They say:
As applied to the brush industry it is unworkable due to the impossibility of tracing the identity of proposed sales tax on raw material through to the manufactured goods. The clerical effort alone necessary to implement this proposal would add to the cost, and the uncertainty of the refunds obtainable would make an addition to our selling price imperative in self protection. The proposal will inevitably increase the cost of goods to the consumer and any gain to the government will be more than offset by the cost of the army of clerks necessary to handle refund claims.
I have other telegrams and letters from people in the lumber business, but the minister no doubt has received these representations and many others besides. The gentleman who sends me that telegram with reference to the brush industry presents his case in a very few lines and I would ask the minister's most careful and favourable consideration for the facts put forward by these respective parties.

Before the minister replies I would like to corroborate what the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) has said. I think we have all received numerous telegrams; I have something like twenty telegrams here from various manufacturing industries throughout Ontario, one of which is a brush industry in Hamilton, similar to the one the hon. member for St. John has just referred to. I have representations also from the Westinghouse Company, and I would like to mention in this connection the case of Dominion Canners. They are large importers of tin plate which they use in the manufacture of cans at their can plant. Their requirements in a year would probably approximate anywhere between a million and a million and a half dollars. To tie up six per cent of this is to deal with no inconsiderable sum, especially

War Revenue Act
when the cans require to remain in their warehouses for a year or two years, or even longer, according to the size of the pack and the conditions of trade. I need not go into the details; I understand that the minister has on the order paper a resolution which is in the shape of an amendment to section 6 of the sales tax bill which will probably meet many of these cases. If so, I do not suppose there is any necessity of my taking up the time of the committee in arguing the twenty or thirty cases I have before me, which are all of the same character.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
All taxes produce criticism. The chief complaint reaching me, however, has been the proposal to tax imports and the argument advanced, as set forth in the communication referred to by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), is that large stocks of goods have to be carried on hand and that the financing involved is a very serious matter. Then the further question is raised in connection with the difficulty involved in the matter of refund. These difficulties are covered by the amendment which I propose to move. With regard to the points mentioned by the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter), only in part can we give relief there. The former tax on lumber was 3 per cent. These various taxes pyramided; you had some imposed at one stage and some at another, and it can be shown by actual transactions that in some of these cases where there was nominally a small tax, the actual tax after it had passed from one stage to another was much higher than 6 per cent. In the case of lumber they paid a special tax of 3 per cent, and I frankly admit they will have to pay now a tax of 6 per cent. I cannot help that; somebody has to get hurt in the matter and I cannot see why lumber should be exempted. No business is very prosperous in Canada to-day, but certainly lumber is not less prosperous than the others; the price of lumber is high and the lumber industry is perhaps well able to bear the burden. The suggestion of the hon. member for St. John City with regard to the date at which some of these things should come into force has, I think, been met, but as to the main question-if it is the main question-namely, that the tax on lumber has been increased from 3 to 6 per cent, I do not see how we can promise any relief on that score. It would be most agreeable to the Minister of Finance if he could make a list of exemptions. Somebody has to get hurt in the readjustment of these taxes. In the end I do not think we shall get much
more money; in fact, I am not aiming at that; the object is to simplify the tax, and if in the end we get any more money, it will not be very much. I think it will be found in a good many cases that the people will pay a smaller tax than they paid before. In regard to housing, there is some force in the suggestions made. If the lumber is imported it can be passed to the manufacturer without the immediate imposition of a tax, but when the lumber is produced at home a tax will have to be paid. That is to say, the saw mill men, those who produce the lumber, will pay the tax; I have no doubt that they will pass it on-although some hon. gentlemen have sought to show that these taxes are not passed on-[DOT] to the contractor, and the contractor will pass it on to the house builder. But I am afraid we cannot help that. Several hon. gentlemen have spoken to me about the telegrams they have been receiving during the last few days, and I think the main difficulty complained of there on this question of the taxing of imports is fully met by the proposed amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
On this matter of the tax on the lumbermen, which the minister has glossed over so gently and respecting which his heart is much moved because the lumberman has to pay, I just wish to say a word or two. The minister has not increased the tax on lumber from 3 to 6 per cent; he has increased it from 2 to 6 per cent. That is what the minister has done in his seventeen months of power. When he came into power there was a lumber sales tax of 2 per cent, because what we use everywhere in Canada for building purposes is our own lumber; and there was no pyramiding allowed-none whatever. The act was as clear as day. It said:
Provided that in respect of lumber an excise tax of 2 per cent shall be imposed, levied and collected on sales and deliveries by the Canadian manufacturer and of 3 per cent on importations, and that no further excise tax shall be payable on re-sale.
That was the law when the minister came into office, and when that law was put on the statute book, hon. gentlemen who are now members of this government headed by the present Prime Minister-in this respect the
War Revenue Act

present Minister of Trade and Commerce was the chief spokesman-denounced the administration for putting a 2 per cent tax on lumber -bewailed the fate of the pioneer, bewailed the fate of the farmer, bewailed the fate of the house builder, to the acclamations of hon. gentlemen of the Progressive party at the time, and called upon us to take the tax off as impossible for the pioneer to bear. And this committee sits quiescent while the present Minister of Finance imposes a tax of 6 per cent on lumber and allows profits on the 6 per cent-profits to the lumber dealer as against the contractor and to the contractor as against the consumer. This the minister has done because, he says, we have to get the money. Well, the House is faced to-night, two or three or four days before prorogation, with a set of estimates almost as big as the estimates that were produced in the middle of the session-estimates, page after page of them, that we ought to have had before us for weeks, even for months, before prorogation. I would like the minister to tell wherein the history of Canada estimates of that magnitude were ever brought down in the last week of the session. Occasionally there would be a single page and that would be all, and there would be a row over that. The members of the present government would then be screaming about the idea of bringing even that much before the House in the dying days of the session. It is unspeakable that this House should be presented with the estimates we are presented with now, running into I do not know how many pages; I have not counted them but it looks like nineteen or twenty pages of estimates entering into new votes and all kinds of votes, increasing salaries here, there and everywhere. Here is presented a second estimate almost equal to the first when we are only three or four days before prorogation, and the minister says we have to tax the settler six per cent on lumber to pay for this. He calls it a tax on the lumberman when it is not a tax on the lumberman at all. He cannot help bur pass on a tax of six per cent. If it is a small tax much of it cannot be passed on, but when it is a large tax of' six per cent all of it is passed. The minister has increased the tax on lumber three hundred per cent, and that is what he has done in respect of many other things. In many other lines he has doubled the tax to the consumer, but in respect of lumber, which is a staple article and has many claims to be within the exemptions, he trebles the tax and then he pleads he has to have the money for purposes of estimates like this presented to the House just three or four

days before we prorogue. Has the minister wholly lost control of his colleagues? His colleagues are completely running away ,/ith the treasury when estimates like these are brought down. I cannot believe the minister is exercising the functions of the Minister of Finance when he allows his colleagues to present to parliament estimates of this character right on the eve of adjournment. Here is $14,711,000 in addition to supplementaries of $5,800,000. We have supplementaries already amounting to over $20,000,000-

on other lines of goods. It would be agreeable to me if I could concur in? that view, but notwithstanding my hon. friend's observations we need the money. The estimates we can discuss at another time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not like to give my hon. friend an assurance that I might not
be able to carry out. Under the act the Governor in Council has power to add to the list of exemptions, but I do not want to give the assurance that that will be done. Is my hon. friend making a plea on behalf of the newspaper publishers as well as the magazine publishers?

No, for the publishers oi magazines and periodical literature. The men engaged in that industry had a right to expect from the resolution that carried unanimously in this House that they would get some relief. I should not like this
bill to pass without a protest on my part. I suppose it is hopeless to look for any change, but certainly what is proposed under this measure seems to be a very heavy tax that will fall upon the consumer. The increase is very great, and I notice that a great deal of discussion centres around, and seems to depend on whether it can be passed on or not. Not enough consideration has been given to those who are to pay the tax after it is passed' on. I listened with care to the words of the leader of the Opposition and I took a note of their purport. I feel that I concur, and must do so, in what he has said in regard to expenditure. In fact after looking over the supplementary estimates that have just been brought down-I am sorry to say this but I feel bound to do so-it does look to me as if the ministers seem to be tumbling over each other to see how they can spend the money. When I look at the long list of items representing the expenditures that has been made in building or repairing harbour improvements or wharves, and when I refer to the further lengthy list of proposed expenditures which has come down, and then think of the vast expenditure in regard to other matters, to say nothing of the increase in the salaries of the deputies, I think that during the two sessions I have spent here I never felt as hopeless as I do to-night. There is just one comment I should like to make on this proposition. I have always been a believer in direct taxation because I thought it was the fairest and most economical form of taxation; in studying out the details of this bill and considering the objections which have been advanced during the discussion I am certainly very much strengthened in my opinion. I do not like this tax. I am not going to discuss it at any length because I know it is futile, but I should like to say this: I do not like it for two or three reasons. One is the inevitable pyramiding which this form of taxation involves. It is absolutely correct, as stated, that the tax will approximate 10 or 11 per cent by the time it is paid by the consumer. That means that the men who pay the taxes actually pay about double the amount the treasury receives, and to my mind it is a rotten form of taxation, if you will excuse the expression. I am not worrying about the manufacturers; I have always found they are very well able to look after themselves. The man I am worrying about is the poor fellow at the other end who finally has to pay the bill. To the manufacturer it is simply a matter of some inconvenience, of, perhaps, extra bookkeeping, and of the tying up of a sum of money for a little time. Eventually the tax is passed on, and the ultimate consumer pays it. He is the man I am worrying about. I should not like this opportunity to pass without repeating the protest I have made before [DOT]against this form of taxation. I do make the appeal to the Finance Minister to consider the matter and see whether he cannot do away, to as great an extent as possible, with this indirect taxation upon commodities which is bound to bear with peculiar hardship upon the consumer by its pyramiding, by the fact that it is not based upon a man's ability to pay but upon the amount of goods he requires to purchase, and must increase in direct ratio to the number of dependents he has in his family. I think we should have it fixed in the House whether a man is taxable or whether he is not. I do not think the parliament has the right to delegate its authority to tax, that is all.

speechtext: Parliament does not delegate any authority at all. It simply gives power to interperet the words.

I am not desirous of
delaying the committee. I understand we are on subclause 3 of 19bbb.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on section 6 generally.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to what perhaps has been overlooked. I do not think there is any objection to this. The suggestion I have to make would properly come on page 5 after the section referring to " sale price " defined. It has reference to concerns which manufacture and retail direct to the people, perhaps dealing more particularly with confectionery, cakes and such like. That is, cases where a bona fide retailer is also a manufacturer. It is claimed by these people that at present the officials of the department presided over by the hon. Minister of Customs and.Inland Revenue determine arbitrarily and without statutory power that the valuation for taxation shall be sixty per cent of the retail price. No objection is taken to that, but it is not provided for in the statute, and the suggestion is made that provision should oe made in the statute for the minister to make regulations in that regard. I have to suggest to the minister an amendment to come in after the word "thereto" in line 8 on page 5 of the bill following the clause that reads:
For the purpose of calculating the amount of the consumption or sales tax, "sale price" shall mean the price before any amount payable in respect of the consumption or sales tax is added thereto.
I propose an amendment to add after the word "thereto" the following:
Provided, however, that the minister may in the case of goods manufactured for sale to the consumer by a person carrying on business exclusively by retail determine by regulation upon what portion of the actual sale price the tax shall be calculated.
War Revenue Act

In other words, that in the case of businesses where a retail manufacturer sells direct to the consumer the minister by regulation shall have the power to fix the price upon which the sales tax shall be applied. If it is provided for already in the bill I would be very glad to have it pointed
12 m. out, but it is pointed out by those more directly interested that the bill does not provide for it at the present time. I know very well that it certainly intended to cover it but I do not think it is covered in the bill. If this amendment is acceptable I would offer it to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
turn to section 13 on page 8 he will find that that is covered. Section 13 reads:
Whenever goods are manufactured or produced in Canada under such circumstances or conditions as render it difficult to determine the value thereof-
That would be the goods described by my hon. friend.
-the minister may determine the value of the tax under this act.
I think that covers the point raised by my hon. friend.

I may say, so that the
minister may understand the spirit in which I bring this forward, that I am quite prepared to accept his assurance that it covers the case if he will so assert, but the information I have is that it does not. At present in the case of a prosecution, for instance, while the interpretation given by many of the officials is that sixty per cent of the retail sale price is the amount upon which the tax
should be levied, there is nothing in the act which authorizes the officials to make that price, and what I am after is that the act shall make it perfectly clear that the officials shall have the authority to fix such a price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under this clause I think they would have the power to fix the price, but not necessarily sixty per cent. I think my hon. friend ought to be willing to leave it to the judgment of the Minister of Customs. I think the words are broad enough, and unless it be found by experience that it does not interpret fairly I do not think the change my hon. friend asks is necessary. I have enough faith in Ministers of Customs, no matter to what government or party they belong, to believe that they are endeavouring to administer the customs and the sales tax laws in a spirit of fairness to all concerned.
I hope my hon. friend will not press his amendment, I think he will find the point is covered.

I might say, so that the minister will correctly interpret my remarks, that I am quite willing to accept his interpretation. That would be the purport of my amendment. If the minister is satisfied that under this clause any regulation made by him or his officials-that would be the Minister of Customs and Excise I understand fixing the value at forty, sixty, seventy or any other percentage is legal, that is what I want to get at. If the minister is satisfied of that my amendment is unnecessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think if the Minister of Customs made a regulation along these lines it would be absolutely certain that he could do so. As to whether it would be wise for him to do so, I would rather leave to his judgment than tie his hands.
In view of that I am quite vailing to accept the minister's interpretation of the act in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thank you.

We had some discussion in connection with the question of 50 per cent. I did not get any answer to my question. Perhaps it is foolish to expect any answer in connection with this bill at all from anybody; but I did ask as to how subsection 7 was going to be worked out; how it was going to be ascertained as to the 50 per cent of the total sales so that this special privilege could be availed of; for how long that 50 per cent would have to continue; and what would happen when the 50 per cent was not maintained.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That I think you will have to leave to the minister.
I am asking, though, a little information from the minister who is here. I suppose the government have some idea of what they are doing by this bill, but I am beginning to think they have not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There were cases in the existing law when it was administered by my hon. friend where the Minister of Customs received large power, and my hon. friend did not see any danger in it at all. The Minister of Customs had power to define this, that and the other thing. My hon. friend did not then imagine any difficulty. I do not see why he should imagine difficulties now.

This is something very different. This bill goes further than any act we ever had.
Mr. FIELDING We had this before.

War Revenue Act
This may seem at first sight a somewhat small thing; but if you take an area like Aylmer, Ontario, or the Okanagan valley, or many other sections where thousands of acres belonging to hundreds of individuals are devoted to the growing of tomatoes, this is an important matter. I would ask the Minister of Customs if it would be possible to do one of two things, either to interpret the act as it, at present stands to include tomato plants, or to make the necessary amendment to include tomato plants in the exemptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the Minister of Customs was dealing with that. I can quite understand, upon all these questions, there may be possibly different rulings by the customs authorities. I really do not know what more the hon. member can do than to leave the matter to the judgment of the minister, and I hope he will give attention to what the hon. member has said. This does not require a change in the bill. If the ruling is wrong, I suppose he will make a ruling to correct it, but I presume he will not admit that it is wrong.
If the very genial and efficient Minister of Customs would intimate that such a ruling would be given, that would be entirely satisfactory.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: A ruling was made by the Commissioner of Customs, and the question was discussed to-day again. My hon. friend says that tomatoes come in free. Supposing apples come in free, would that necessarily make the tree free?
The act makes the tree free and also the fruit of the tree.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: One might go further. If milk came in free would you allow the cow m free?

The cow being a milk factory, I do not think the case is a parallel one.
, Mr. BUREAU: The matter is under consideration, under an appeal from the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie).
Can the minister give some assurance?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: I cannot give an assurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hope, not assurance.
This "hope" business is l ather discouraging at times. I see* in the countenance of the Minister of Customs, some ray of, might I say, new hope reflected.
That means nothing. I have had experience.

I was unable to get any information as to the clause relating to jobbers. If I cannot get any information from the ministers, I want to give them a little information which, I think, can fairly be considered in connection with this matter. I point out that a distinction is made between classes of jobbers, and that it is unfair to make a distinction between classes. I point out that business of the same character should be dealt with on a similar basis. I point out that the licensed jobber will be relieved of any burden as to refunds and such troubles and that he does not have to finance the tax on his purchases. The unlicensed jobber has to finance his tax, and in order to sell to the licensed manufacturer he must be in a position to know from whom he purchased the goods shipped; and he must keep his stocks separate. This is a very difficult matter in connection with bulk goods. The unlicensed jobber must also know when the goods were purchased and the prices paid. The government will have to keep a check on all this if we are to have anything like equitable treatment between the two classes. I have been met by the government with the statement that they cannot give any information, but I hope they will endeavour to inform themselves on the subject before they attempt to enforce this measure. I trust that something will be done to preserve a semblance of fairness in the matter. Is it possible to make these refunds? The minister cannot tell me anything about his machinery, but perhaps when we come to some of the other sections he may be able to ascertain from his deputy how the department will arrive at the amount of refunds that have to be made between now and the first of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that there are not likely to be any refunds in the way my hon. friend describes, but there will be deductions.
The matter can only be adjusted by means of stocktaking. Who is to take the stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The man owning the goods will have to be prepared to show a stock record. All these things are matters to be determined by conference between the parties concerned and the department, and I do not anticipate the difficulty which my hon. friend seems to apprehend.

There is only one way of checking up these deductions or refunds, whatever you choose to call them.
War Revenue Act

Any business man will tell my hon. friend that the only way of keeping a check on the matter is to take stock of the goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In a hundred cases the departments have to check up statements, and I presume the same thing will be done in this case. The officials of the department will have to check up the statements of the party wherever necessary.
In other words, the man takes stock and the department checks his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Has the minister any idea as to what that will cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It is quite right that these deductions should be made in respect of unmanufactured goods, but why should not similar deductions be made in the case of manufactured goods unsold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understand that the
same rule will apply in that case; there is no difference.

The section is
exceedingly long and I do not see how anybody can read it in one breath and get the sense of it. If the minister says that it covers the completed article I am satisfied; but so far as I can see, it refers only to articles that must be further manufactured. If I am wrong the minister will correct me.
If the importer does not pay any duty where does the refund come in? How can there be a refund if no duty has been paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If a duty has been paid the manufacturer is clearly entitled to a refund, but obviously there would be no deduction if no duty had been paid.
This therefore would apply to goods already imported. It could not apply to goods to be imported in the future.
I should be glad if the minister would clear up the point I have already raised. Does this refund apply to the finished article which is still on hand?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the manufacturer has paid the tax he is entitled to the refund.
Then we have it definite; the refund or deduction or repayment will apply to the finished article just as much as to the raw material.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they have paid the 5 per cent.
Yes; but everything now has to pay the 6 per cent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-Failure or refusal to keep books.

There is an anomaly in this section. Subsection 19b reads:
19e. If a manufacturer or producer fails or refuses to keep adequate books or accounts, in English or French, for the purposes of this act, the minister may, by notice in writing, require the manufacturer or producer to keep such records and accounts as the minister may prescribe.
I would suggest that we strike out the words, "in English or French" because otherwise it would mean that a manufacturer or producer might keep books in any other language- Choctaw or Iroquois, for instance-and could not be proceeded against.
I do not think my hon. friend is correctly reading the section. It means that the use of the Choctaw language would be an offence.
Why not strike it out altogether?
Then Choctaw would be good. My hon. friend does not understand Choctaw.	Ik

Nor do I understand this section very clearly. If a man does not know either English or French, and keeps his accounts in Spanish or Italian, it ought to be a very simple matter for the department to find out whether his books are properly kept or not. He ought not to be penalized if he cannot keep his books in English or French.
That is another argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If you are going to make an active requirement that the accounts should be kept, I think it is right to specify English or French. I do not agree with my hon. friend that Choctaw could be used.

I think some consideration should be given to the suggestion of my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). Our English and French ancestors acquired this country by achieving mastery over the people for whom my hon. friend pleads. The minister might perhaps consent to an amendment to permit the use of English, French or Choctaw-and then my hon. friend's objection would be met.

War Revenue Act

As my hon. friend has
helped me out of the hole, I would suggest that he include Micmac, which I understand is current in New Brunswick.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subsection agreed to.
On section 8, subsection 19g-Refund on goods sold to province if province exempt from tax.
Why should this refund be made? 1 always understood my hon. friend required the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The object of this, I am advised, is that a local government, for example, could import an article free of duty, but in the case of a manufacturer or producer producing the same article he would be subject to tax. In that case when he sells to the local government he could get a refund so he would be put on even terms with the importer.

This shows the infinity of trouble my hon. friend is making for himself. I thought it was bad enough when we had a lot of refunds at the commencement, but now apparently claims can be put in anywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are all there for a good purpose.
I do not see why the principle that underlies the exemption of provincial governments should not be extended to municipal governments as well or else be denied to all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under the British North America Act I am afraid we cannot tax the Crown, that is, a provincial government, but we can tax a municipality. That is the ground of the difference.

I think in cases under the Income Tax Act as to questions of priorities and the like we had the general right of taxing fairly well settled. As to the liquor case in British Columbia my recollection is that the Privy Council decided that we had the right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For resale.
We put it on resale in that case. Does my hon. friend suggest that the provinces have not to pay customs tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is one of the interesting constitutional questions that arise in Canada. We are advised that in all probability we have not the right to impose the tax on provincial governments unless they have the goods for resale.
I think to-day we are taxing for customs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a nice legal question to put it mildly and I do not think we ought to put a tax on the provinces which would involve us in difficulties.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subsection agreed to.
Section agreed to.
On section 10-Government or provincial sales; use of postage stamps.
What does that refer to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Subsection 3 of section
19 is the clause which permits the use of postage stamps, which after a given date are no longer to be used.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-Schedule 1 amended.

What is the
effect of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The passages struck out relate to confectionery and beverages, which were the subject of discussion before.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to direct your attention to a defect in the French translation of the bill. In the English version, in the 25th line of subsection 8 of section 6, the words appear, "no deduction to be allowed in respect of such goods not accounted for prior to the thirty-first day of March, 1924." These words are translated as follows: "aucune remise ne devant etre accordee con-cernant des marchandises possedees." The word "possedees" means on hand; it should be replaced by the proper French translation of the English words, "not accounted for."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend having
called attention to the defect in the translation, I have no doubt that it will be remedied.
